body: In V.B. Rangaraj v V.B. Gopalakrishnan (1992) the Supreme Court held that a restriction on transferring shares binds the company and shareholders only if it is in the articles. That is why term sheets require the SHA’s transfer clauses (right of first refusal, tag-along, drag-along, lock-ins) and investor affirmative votes to be copied into the articles.

Later courts softened this for private bargains between particular shareholders: the Bombay High Court in Messer Holdings v Shyam Madanmohan Ruia (2010) enforced a consensual arrangement between specific shareholders about their own shares. The practical rule has not changed: mirror the SHA in the articles.

When founders fall out, minority holders can petition the NCLT for oppression and mismanagement under sections 241–242. In Tata Consultancy Services v Cyrus Investments (2021) the Supreme Court held that removing an executive chairman is not oppression by itself and that the NCLT cannot reinstate a removed director. NCLTs have also refused to send oppression petitions to arbitration just because the SHA has an arbitration clause.
keyPoints: Copy SHA transfer restrictions into the articles
Oppression remedies sit with the NCLT, not an arbitrator
Board removal is not oppression by itself (Tata v Mistry)

sources.t: Tata v Cyrus (SC, 2021) on Indian Kanoon
Bar & Bench on USAR Commerce v Utsav Soi

lessons.summary: Investor rights that restrict share transfers are safest when written into the articles of association.
lessons.title: Shareholders’ agreements, the articles, and founder fights
lessons.plain: Founders and investors sign a shareholders' agreement (SHA). Indian courts say rules about selling shares only bind everyone if they are also written into the company's own rulebook (the articles). So copy them there. If founders fight, unhappy shareholders go to a special tribunal (the NCLT). Being removed from the board is not, by itself, 'unfair treatment' in law.

body: Section 27 makes any agreement in restraint of a lawful trade void, with a narrow exception for the sale of goodwill. Courts read it strictly. A restraint during employment is valid (Niranjan Shankar Golikari v Century Spinning, 1967), but a restraint after the contract ends is void (Superintendence Co. v Krishan Murgai, 1980; Percept D’Mark v Zaheer Khan, 2006).

Founders and employees can therefore be bound by exclusivity while they work for the company, by confidentiality forever, and by garden-leave arrangements, but a clause stopping them from working for a competitor after they leave will generally fail. Courts have been more willing to enforce narrow non-solicitation of clients and staff, but the law is not settled.

IP: under the Copyright Act, work made by an employee in the course of employment belongs to the employer, but work by consultants, freelancers and founders before incorporation does not. Get written assignments (section 19) from everyone else, including founders for pre-incorporation code.
keyPoints: Post-exit non-competes are void under s.27
In-term exclusivity and confidentiality are enforceable
Get written IP assignments from founders and contractors

sources.t: Percept D’Mark v Zaheer Khan on Indian Kanoon

lessons.summary: Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act voids post-exit non-competes; in-term restraints and confidentiality are enforceable.
lessons.title: Non-competes, non-solicits and who owns the IP
lessons.plain: A clause saying 'you can't work for a competitor after you leave' is generally not enforceable in India. But while you still work for the company, you can be told to work only for it, and to keep secrets forever. Code written by freelancers or by founders before the company existed is not automatically the company's: get it signed over in writing.

body: Two Indian parties may choose a foreign seat, and the award is enforced as a foreign award (PASL Wind Solutions v GE Power Conversion, 2021). An emergency arbitrator’s order under SIAC rules in an India-seated arbitration is enforceable (Amazon v Future Retail, 2021).

A seven-judge bench in December 2023 held that an unstamped or under-stamped agreement is inadmissible until stamp duty is paid but is not void, so the arbitration clause survives (In re Interplay). A Constitution Bench the same month accepted the group-of-companies doctrine, so non-signatory group entities can be bound where the parties intended it (Cox and Kings v SAP India).

Resisting a foreign award in India is hard: the public-policy ground is narrow (Vijay Karia, 2020). In Nagaraj V. Mylandla v PI Opportunities Fund-I (25 March 2026) the Supreme Court enforced a Singapore-seated SIAC award against promoters who had failed to give investors the exit promised in their shareholders’ agreement, and recognised transnational issue estoppel.
keyPoints: Indian parties can pick a foreign seat
Emergency arbitrator orders are enforceable
Unstamped ≠ void (2023)
Exit promises to investors are enforced (Nagaraj Mylandla, 2026)
lessons.summary: Most funding documents use SIAC or another institution; Supreme Court rulings since 2020 make those clauses work in India.
lessons.title: Arbitration: foreign seats, emergency relief, stamps and non-signatories
lessons.plain: Many investment contracts send disputes to private arbitration, often in Singapore. Indian courts now back this strongly: they enforce emergency orders, foreign awards and investor exit promises. A paperwork slip like unpaid stamp duty doesn't kill the arbitration clause, but you still have to pay the duty.

body: The Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 were notified on 13 November 2025 (published 14 November). Provisions setting up the Data Protection Board took effect immediately.
Phase 2 began on 13 November 2026: consent managers must register with the Board (Rule 4). If you are not applying to be a consent manager, nothing new is required of you yet.

Phase 3 starts 13 May 2027: notice and consent, security safeguards, breach intimation to the Board and affected users, retention and erasure, children’s data, data principal rights, significant data fiduciary duties and cross-border transfer conditions. Penalties under the Act go up to ₹250 crore per breach for failing to take reasonable security safeguards.
keyPoints: 13 Nov 2025: Board set up
13 Nov 2026: consent-manager registration
13 May 2027: core obligations
Max penalty ₹250 crore
lessons.summary: Most obligations bite on 13 May 2027.
lessons.title: DPDP Act 2023 and Rules 2025: the compliance clock
lessons.plain: India's data-protection law tells businesses how to handle people's personal data. It is switching on in stages. Most duties, like getting proper consent, keeping data safe and reporting leaks, start on 13 May 2027. Big penalties apply if you don't take reasonable security steps.

body: The Code on Wages 2019, Industrial Relations Code 2020, Code on Social Security 2020 and Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code 2020 took effect on 21 November 2025. Central and state rules are still being finalised on some points.
A uniform definition of ‘wages’ applies: if allowances exceed 50% of total pay, the excess is added back to wages. That raises provident fund and gratuity costs for startups that kept basic pay low.

Fixed-term employees get the same benefits as permanent staff and become eligible for gratuity after one year instead of five. Aggregators must contribute 1–2% of turnover, capped at 5% of payouts to gig and platform workers, towards their social security.
keyPoints: Wages must be at least 50% of remuneration
Fixed-term gratuity after 1 year
Aggregator contribution for gig workers
lessons.summary: 29 central labour laws were replaced; salary structures and fixed-term contracts changed most.
lessons.title: The four labour codes (in force 21 November 2025)
lessons.plain: Four new labour laws replaced many old ones in November 2025. The big change for startups: at least half of an employee's pay must count as 'wages'. That raises provident fund and gratuity costs. Fixed-term staff now get gratuity after one year, and app platforms must contribute to gig workers' social security.

body: Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 protects intermediaries from liability for third-party content if they observe due diligence and act on actual knowledge. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India (2015) the Supreme Court read ‘actual knowledge’ as a court order or government notification, and struck down section 66A.

Platforms that take an active role can lose the shield: in Christian Louboutin v Nakul Bajaj (2018) the Delhi High Court held that an e-commerce site that actively curates, stores and promotes products may not be a mere intermediary.
The IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 add grievance officers and takedown timelines; larger social-media intermediaries have extra duties.
keyPoints: Safe harbour needs due diligence and passivity
Actual knowledge = court order or government notice
Active curation can forfeit protection
lessons.summary: Marketplaces and apps rely on section 79, which protects only passive intermediaries.
lessons.title: Platforms and safe harbour under the IT Act
lessons.plain: Apps and marketplaces are usually not blamed for what their users post or sell (this is called safe harbour), if they follow the rules. They must act when a court or the government tells them to. But a platform that actively selects, stores and promotes products can lose that protection.

body: DPIIT notification G.S.R. 108(E) dated 4 February 2026 replaced the 19 February 2019 notification. A regular startup must be within 10 years of incorporation or registration and its turnover must not have exceeded ₹200 crore in any financial year (up from ₹100 crore).

A new Deep Tech Startup category allows up to 20 years from incorporation and a ₹300 crore turnover ceiling, for entities working on novel, IP-heavy technology with long development cycles. Cooperative societies are now eligible alongside private limited companies, LLPs and registered partnerships. Entities formed by splitting up or reconstructing an existing business do not qualify.
Recognition does not by itself give the tax holiday: that needs a separate certificate from the Inter-Ministerial Board, and the tax holiday’s own turnover cap stays at ₹100 crore.
keyPoints: Regular startup: ≤10 years, turnover ≤₹200 crore in every year
Deep Tech Startup: ≤20 years, turnover ≤₹300 crore
Tax-holiday turnover cap remains ₹100 crore
Splits and reconstructions are excluded
lessons.summary: Recognition is the gateway to most startup-specific benefits, and its definition changed on 4 February 2026.
lessons.title: What counts as a ‘startup’: the DPIIT 2026 framework
lessons.plain: The government can give your company an official 'startup' label. With it you get special relaxations. Since February 2026, a normal startup must be under 10 years old with sales that never crossed ₹200 crore in a year. Deep-tech startups get longer and bigger limits. The label alone does not give you the tax holiday; that needs a separate approval.

body: A private limited company can issue equity and preference shares, run an ESOP plan and receive foreign investment under the automatic route in most sectors, which is why investors expect it. An LLP cannot issue shares or share-based ESOPs, and foreign investment in LLPs is limited to sectors open 100% under the automatic route without performance conditions.
A One Person Company suits a solo founder testing an idea. Since 2021 an OPC can convert to a private or public company at any time, and NRIs can incorporate one.

A ‘small company’ gets lighter compliance (for example, only two board meetings a year and no cash-flow statement). MCA rules effective 1 December 2025 raised the limits to paid-up capital up to ₹10 crore and turnover up to ₹100 crore. The Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026, introduced on 23 March 2026, would raise the statutory ceiling to ₹20 crore and ₹200 crore; a Joint Parliamentary Committee reported on it on 3 August 2026 and it still has to be passed.
keyPoints: Raise VC money through a private limited company
LLPs cannot issue ESOP shares
Small company: ≤₹10 crore paid-up and ≤₹100 crore turnover (since 1 Dec 2025)
₹20 crore / ₹200 crore ceilings are only proposed

sources.t: Business Today on MCA rules, Dec 2025

lessons.summary: Venture capital almost always expects a private limited company.
lessons.title: Choosing the entity: private company, LLP or OPC
lessons.plain: Before you start, you choose what kind of business to form. If you want investors, form a private limited company: it can issue shares and ESOPs. An LLP is simpler but cannot issue shares. A One Person Company suits a solo founder testing an idea.

body: Fresh shares go out by private placement (section 42, with offers to at most 200 persons a year excluding qualified institutional buyers and ESOP employees), preferential allotment (section 62(1)(c), special resolution and a registered valuer’s report) or a rights issue.

ESOPs are issued under section 62(1)(b) and Rule 12 of the Share Capital and Debentures Rules: at least one year between grant and vesting, and normally no grants to promoters or to directors holding more than 10%. A startup may grant ESOPs to its promoters and such directors for up to 10 years from incorporation.

Sweat equity (section 54) is normally capped, but a startup may issue sweat equity up to 50% of its paid-up capital for up to 10 years from incorporation. A DPIIT-recognised startup may also accept a convertible note of at least ₹25 lakh in a single tranche, repayable or convertible within 10 years, without it counting as a deposit.
keyPoints: ESOP minimum vesting: 1 year
Startups may give ESOPs to promoters for 10 years from incorporation
Sweat equity up to 50% of paid-up capital in the first 10 years
Convertible note: ≥₹25 lakh, single tranche, 10-year window

sources.t: Indian Kanoon: Companies Act 2013, s.62 and s.54

lessons.summary: The Companies Act gives startups specific relaxations on employee equity and early funding.
lessons.title: Shares, ESOPs, sweat equity and convertible notes
lessons.plain: This lesson covers the ways a company can hand out ownership. It can sell new shares to chosen people, give employees options (ESOPs), or give shares for work instead of cash (sweat equity). Startups get special freedom here in their first 10 years, for example founders can receive ESOPs.

body: Control has four layers: economic ownership (who gets the money), voting power (who wins shareholder votes), the board (who appoints and removes the CEO), and reserved matters (lists of decisions that need a particular investor’s consent). Investors negotiate hardest for the last two. Uber’s 2017 fight was about who could fill board seats, not about share percentages.

Tools available to a private Indian company: founder nominee board seats written into the articles and tied to a holding threshold; founder reserved matters (you can ask for your own veto list, not just investors’); a voting agreement or common holding company so co-founders vote as a block; and shares with differential voting rights under section 43 and Rule 4 of the Share Capital Rules, which may not exceed 74% of total voting power and must be permitted by the articles and approved by shareholders.

At IPO, SEBI’s superior voting rights framework (2019, relaxed in 2021) lets founders of technology-intensive companies list while holding shares with 2:1 to 10:1 votes, subject to a sunset (5 years, extendable by 5), coattail matters where SR shares vote 1:1, and a 74% cap on SR voting. In 2021 SEBI noted no company had used it.
keyPoints: Watch the board and the veto list more than the cap table
Put founder board seats in the articles
DVR shares: up to 74% of voting power
SEBI SR shares at IPO: 2:1–10:1, sunset clause

sources.t: SEBI board memo on SR shares (2021)
Deccan Herald on SEBI SR framework

lessons.summary: Founders usually lose control through the board and reserved matters long before they fall below 50% of the shares.
lessons.title: Control = votes + board seats + vetoes, not just shares
lessons.plain: Owning most of the shares is not the same as being in control. Real control comes from who sits on the board and who can veto decisions. Founders usually lose control there first. You can protect yourself with board seats written into the articles, your own veto list, voting together with co-founders, or shares with extra votes.

body: Anthropic is a public benefit corporation. Its Long-Term Benefit Trust holds Class T stock, which has no economic rights but elects directors who together form a majority of the board. According to the IPO filing of 26 October 2026 as reported, the seven co-founders hold Class F supervoting stock that carries a majority of the general shareholder vote and elects the remaining directors; once Class F is gone, the board becomes staggered. So the founders do hold a majority of shareholder votes, but the board majority belongs to the independent Trust, not to them.

Facebook went public with Mark Zuckerberg controlling about 60% of the vote through Class B shares. In 2016 it tried to add non-voting Class C shares so he could sell stock for charity without losing control. Minority shareholders sued in the Delaware Court of Chancery and Facebook dropped the plan in September 2017, days before Zuckerberg was due to testify.

WeWork’s Adam Neumann planned shares with 20 votes each. The 2019 IPO filing exposed governance problems, he resigned, the IPO was withdrawn, and WeWork filed for bankruptcy in November 2023. Supervoting shares did not protect him from investors who controlled the money.
keyPoints: Design control before outside money comes in
Give it a purpose, limits and a sunset
Changing rules later as controller = fiduciary lawsuit risk
Supervoting can’t fix bad governance

sources.t: Law.com on Facebook dropping Class C

lessons.summary: Lock in control at the start, explain why, and give it limits; changing the rules later as the controller invites lawsuits.
lessons.title: Control structures compared: Anthropic, Facebook, WeWork
lessons.plain: Three companies show different ways to handle founder control. Anthropic set up an independent trust that controls the board. Facebook tried to change its share rules later to keep Zuckerberg in control, and dropped the plan after a lawsuit. WeWork's founder had extra-vote shares but was still pushed out. Lesson: set control rules early, explain why, and give them limits.

body: Sort every clause into two piles. Economics: valuation, liquidation preference, anti-dilution, option pool, dividends. Control: board composition, reserved matters, drag-along, transfer restrictions, information rights, founder vesting and leaver terms, exclusivity, and exit obligations (put options, buybacks, IPO deadlines).

Model the exit waterfall at three outcomes (a fire sale, a modest exit, a big win). Preferences and anti-dilution only bite in bad and middling outcomes, which are the most likely ones. Then list every obligation that falls on you personally rather than on the company.

In India, a foreign investor’s exit option is allowed only without an assured return and after at least a one-year lock-in (FEMA). But investors still enforce exit promises: in Nagaraj Mylandla (2026) the Supreme Court enforced a Singapore award against promoters who had not delivered the exit they promised. Check the governing law and seat of arbitration before signing.
keyPoints: Two piles: economics and control
Model the waterfall in bad, middling and good exits
List obligations on you personally
FEMA: no assured-return exits for foreign investors
lessons.summary: Most founders negotiate valuation and miss the clauses that decide who walks away with what.
lessons.title: Reading a term sheet: separate the money from the control
lessons.plain: When reading an investor's offer, sort each clause into two piles: money (valuation, who gets paid first) and control (board seats, vetoes, forced sales). Then work out what you would actually get if the company sells for little, for a medium price, or for a lot. Watch for any promise that you, personally, must keep.

body: GoMechanic’s founders admitted misreporting in January 2023 when SoftBank-led diligence found problems; 70% of staff were laid off and police later filed an FIR alleging funds were siphoned. Zilingo’s CEO was terminated in 2022 after an investor-commissioned investigation. BharatPe removed its managing director in 2022 and sued him and his family, alleging misappropriation, before settling in 2024. In Byju’s US case, a court entered a default judgment in 2025 because of the founder’s failure to comply with discovery orders, later reopened on damages.

The rules: never inflate revenue or users; route every transaction with founders, relatives or your other companies through section 188 approvals at arm’s length; keep personal and company money separate; minute every board decision; hire an independent finance head and a credible auditor; set up a whistleblower channel; buy D&O insurance; and always comply with court orders, even ones you plan to appeal.
Due diligence for the next round is where most problems surface. Assume every number you send an investor will be audited later.
keyPoints: Diligence finds what the founder hides
Related-party deals need s.188 approvals
Comply with court orders while you challenge them
Separate personal and company money
lessons.summary: Indian founder blow-ups of 2022–26 share a pattern: numbers, money flows and records that could not survive scrutiny.
lessons.title: Governance hygiene that keeps founders out of court
lessons.plain: Many Indian founders got into legal trouble because their numbers or money trails could not survive checking. Never inflate figures. Keep personal and company money separate. Get proper approval for deals with yourself, your relatives or your other companies. Keep records of every decision, and obey court orders even while you appeal them.

body: Investor SHAs usually require founders to work full time on the company and not to start or join other businesses. That restraint is enforceable while you remain a founder-employee (Golikari, 1967), even though a post-exit non-compete is void under section 27. Negotiate a schedule listing your other ventures and a carve-out for non-competing businesses before the first institutional round.

As a director you must avoid conflicts and undue gain (section 166), disclose your interest in other companies (section 184), and get approval for transactions between your companies on arm’s-length terms (section 188). Each company should own its own IP; do not reuse code or brand assets across companies without a written licence. You can be a director of at most 20 companies, of which at most 10 public (section 165).

Contagion is real: if one company fails to file financial statements or annual returns for three consecutive years, its directors are disqualified for five years from directorships in other companies too (section 164(2)). A holding company or family investment company can hold your stakes cleanly, but note the 2026 buyback rules tax ‘promoters’ more.
keyPoints: Negotiate carve-outs for your other ventures early
Disclose interests; approve related-party deals
Each company owns its IP
One company’s filing defaults can disqualify you everywhere
lessons.summary: Plan conflicts, exclusivity and liability before the second company exists.
lessons.title: Running several startups in different industries
lessons.plain: Investors usually want founders to work only on their company. If you plan several startups, negotiate permission for your other ventures before taking money. Disclose your interests, keep each company's IP separate, and keep every company's filings up to date: one company's missed filings can bar you from being a director everywhere.

body: Watch for: auditor resignation or a qualified audit opinion; late filings on the MCA portal; a lender declaring default or accelerating a loan; an investor’s nominee resigning from the board or a sudden change in board size; an investor marking down its stake; an oppression petition under sections 241–242 or an insolvency petition under the IBC; whistleblower complaints; and senior finance staff leaving.

For your own companies, treat these as fire alarms: call a board meeting, get independent advice, document everything, and communicate with investors before they hear it elsewhere. Disputes that settle early (BharatPe took over two years) cost far less.
This library tracks live founder disputes in the Founder playbook and updates them daily, so you can see how each fight develops and which moves work.
keyPoints: Auditor exits and late filings are red flags
Lender default notices escalate fast
Act early: board meeting, advice, records
lessons.summary: Founder disputes usually show public signals months before the headline.
lessons.title: Spotting a fight early: warning signals
lessons.plain: Founder fights usually show warning signs months before the news breaks. Watch for: the auditor quitting, filings running late, a lender declaring default, an investor's board member resigning, or legal petitions. If you see these in your own company, act early: call a board meeting, get advice and keep records.

body: Equity instruments for foreign investors are equity shares, fully and mandatorily convertible preference shares (CCPS) and debentures (CCDs), and share warrants. Anything optionally convertible or redeemable is treated as debt and falls under external commercial borrowing rules. That is why Indian VC rounds use CCPS.

Pricing: a non-resident must not get shares below fair value (by an internationally accepted method, certified by a chartered accountant or SEBI-registered merchant banker); on transfers, a resident cannot sell to a non-resident below fair value and a non-resident cannot sell to a resident above it.

The US SAFE is not a recognised instrument in India. Indian ‘iSAFE’ notes are usually structured as CCPS. A DPIIT-recognised startup can instead issue a convertible note of at least ₹25 lakh to a non-resident. Report foreign allotments in Form FC-GPR within 30 days and transfers in Form FC-TRS within 60 days on the RBI FIRMS portal.
keyPoints: Use CCPS/CCDs, not optionally convertible instruments, for foreign money
Issue to non-residents at or above fair value
FC-GPR: 30 days; FC-TRS: 60 days

sources.t: Indian Kanoon: FEMA Non-Debt Instruments Rules, 2019

lessons.summary: Foreign money must come in as equity instruments under the FEMA Non-Debt Instruments Rules, 2019.
lessons.title: Instruments: equity, CCPS, CCDs, convertible notes and ‘iSAFEs’
lessons.plain: Foreign investors can only put money into Indian startups in certain forms that count as ownership, which is why Indian deals use CCPS. They can't pay less than a fair, officially calculated price. The US-style SAFE isn't recognised in India. You must report foreign investment to the RBI within set deadlines.

body: Press Note 3 of 2020 requires government approval for any investment by an entity of a country sharing a land border with India (Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, China, Myanmar, Nepal, Pakistan), or where the beneficial owner is in or a citizen of such a country. Even one Chinese limited partner in a global fund could trigger it.

On 10 March 2026 the Cabinet approved amendments (issued as Press Note 2 of 2026). Investors located outside land-border countries whose land-border beneficial ownership is up to 10% and non-controlling can now use the automatic route. Investors based in land-border countries still need approval.
Before closing a round with a global fund, ask for a beneficial-ownership declaration and check whether the 10% non-controlling test is met.
keyPoints: Direct LBC investors still need approval
≤10% non-controlling LBC ownership via non-LBC investors: automatic route (2026)
Get beneficial-ownership declarations from funds
lessons.summary: Money with a land-border-country link needed government approval from April 2020; March 2026 relaxed the indirect case.
lessons.title: Press Note 3 and its 2026 easing
lessons.plain: Since 2020, money linked to countries bordering India (like China) needs government approval before it can be invested. In 2026 the rule was relaxed. Investors based elsewhere whose land-border owners hold a small, non-controlling stake (up to 10%) no longer need approval. Always ask global funds who their real owners are.

body: Section 68 of the Companies Act caps a buyback at 25% of paid-up capital plus free reserves, needs a special resolution (a board resolution suffices up to 10%), allows only one buyback in 12 months, and requires debt not to exceed twice capital and free reserves afterwards. The Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 would let prescribed classes of companies go beyond 25%.

Tax changed again on 1 April 2026: buyback proceeds are taxed as capital gains, with an additional tax on promoters (see the Tax volume). Secondary sales to new investors are the usual alternative; check FEMA pricing if a non-resident buys from a resident.
For ESOP liquidity, many startups run periodic buybacks or arrange secondaries with incoming investors.
keyPoints: Buyback cap: 25% of paid-up capital + free reserves
One buyback per 12 months
From 1 April 2026: capital gains plus promoter add-on tax
lessons.summary: Buybacks give ESOP holders and angels liquidity, but company law and tax both limit them.
lessons.title: Exits for early holders: buybacks and secondaries
lessons.plain: Early shareholders and employees often want to turn shares into cash before any big sale. Companies can buy shares back (within legal limits, and once a year), or new investors can buy existing shares (a secondary sale). Since April 2026, buyback money is taxed as capital gains, with extra tax for promoters.

body: The Income-tax Act, 2025 came into force on 1 April 2026 and applies from tax year 2026-27. It replaces ‘previous year’ and ‘assessment year’ with a single ‘tax year’ and has 536 sections in 23 chapters. Income up to 31 March 2026 is still governed by the 1961 Act, so disputes about older years use old section numbers.

Useful mappings for startups: the startup tax holiday (old s.80-IAC) is now section 140; loss carry-forward on change of shareholding (old ss.78–79) is section 119; the gift-type charge on under-priced receipts (old s.56(2)(x)) is section 92(2)(m); old s.80C is section 123. The angel-tax provision (old s.56(2)(viib)) has no counterpart.
Practical step: ESOP plans, SHAs, employment contracts and tax opinions that cite 1961 section numbers should be updated.
keyPoints: In force 1 April 2026; single ‘tax year’
Old Act still governs tax year 2025-26 and earlier
lessons.summary: The 1961 Act was replaced; rates mostly carried over, section numbers did not.
lessons.title: The Income-tax Act, 2025: what changed on 1 April 2026
lessons.plain: India replaced its 1961 income-tax law with a new Income-tax Act, 2025 from 1 April 2026. Tax rates mostly stayed the same, but almost every section number changed, and 'previous year/assessment year' became one 'tax year'. Update any documents that quote old section numbers.

body: An eligible startup can deduct all its profits for three consecutive years of its choice within the first ten years from incorporation. It must be a DPIIT-recognised company or LLP, hold a certificate from the Inter-Ministerial Board, have turnover up to ₹100 crore, and be incorporated before 1 April 2030.

The trade-off: a company that opts for the 22% concessional corporate rate (old s.115BAA) gives up Chapter VI-A deductions such as this holiday. Most startups are loss-making in early years, so the right choice is to time the three-year window for when profits arrive and model it against the concessional rate.
Apply for the IMB certificate early; it is not automatic with DPIIT recognition.
keyPoints: 3 consecutive years out of first 10
Turnover ≤₹100 crore; incorporated before 1 April 2030
Needs IMB certificate
Not combinable with the 22% concessional regime
lessons.summary: 100% of profits deductible for any 3 consecutive years out of the first 10, if you qualify.
lessons.title: The startup tax holiday (old s.80-IAC, new s.140)
lessons.plain: An eligible startup can pay zero income tax on its profits for any 3 years in a row of its choice, within its first 10 years. It needs a separate government certificate and sales under ₹100 crore. Since most startups make losses early, pick the 3 years when profits arrive.

body: At exercise, the difference between fair market value and the exercise price is a salary perquisite taxed at the employee’s slab rate. At sale, the gain over that fair market value is capital gains. For unlisted shares held more than 24 months, long-term gains are taxed at 12.5% without indexation (since 23 July 2024); shorter holdings are taxed at slab rates.

Employees of startups eligible for the tax holiday can defer tax on the perquisite until the earliest of: 48 months from the end of the relevant assessment year, sale of the shares, or leaving the company. Budget 2026 did not change ESOP taxation.
For the company, the ESOP discount is deductible as an employee cost: the Karnataka High Court so held in CIT v Biocon (2020).
keyPoints: Tax at exercise (salary) and at sale (capital gains)
Unlisted LTCG: >24 months, 12.5%
Deferral up to 48 months for eligible startups
Company can deduct ESOP cost (Biocon)

sources.t: Treelife: Income Tax Act 2025 is live

lessons.summary: Employees are taxed at exercise and again at sale; eligible startups can defer the first charge.
lessons.title: ESOP tax and the startup deferral
lessons.plain: With ESOPs, employees are taxed twice: first when they buy the shares (the discount counts as salary), and again when they sell (the profit counts as capital gains). Staff at eligible startups can delay the first tax. The company can treat ESOP cost as a business expense.

body: For a closely held company, business losses can be carried forward only if shareholders holding at least 51% of voting power on the last day of the year of loss still hold it on the last day of the year of set-off (old s.79, now s.119 of the 2025 Act). Large primary rounds, secondaries and buybacks can break this.

Eligible startups get an alternative test for losses from the first 10 years: losses survive if all shareholders who held shares on the last day of the year of loss still hold those shares, even if dilution means they now hold less than 51%.
Planning point: before a secondary sale or buyback, check whether any original shareholder will exit entirely, because that can fail the startup test.
keyPoints: 51% continuity test for closely held companies
Startup alternative: all loss-year shareholders keep their shares
Secondaries can wipe out tax losses
lessons.summary: Closely held companies lose carried-forward losses when control changes, with a relaxation for startups.
lessons.title: Keeping your losses through funding rounds
lessons.plain: A company's past losses can usually reduce tax on its future profits. But for private companies, if ownership changes too much, those losses can be lost. Eligible startups get an easier test: losses survive as long as all the original shareholders still hold their shares. So check before an early shareholder sells out completely.

body: Buybacks were once a way for unlisted companies to return cash without dividend distribution tax. The government responded with a 20% tax on the company for unlisted buybacks (s.115QA, 2013), extended to listed companies in 2019.

From 1 October 2024 the whole buyback receipt became a deemed dividend in the shareholder’s hands, with the cost of shares left as a capital loss. Finance Act 2026 reversed this from 1 April 2026: buyback proceeds are capital gains for all shareholders, and promoters pay an additional tax so that the effective rate is 22% for corporate promoters and 30% for non-corporate promoters.

Commentators have flagged that the promoter definition may catch founders and large holders in startups (reports cite holders above 10%). For employees and small angels, buybacks are now taxed only on the actual gain.
keyPoints: Till Sep 2024: company paid buyback tax
Oct 2024–Mar 2026: deemed dividend for shareholders
From 1 Apr 2026: capital gains; promoters 22%/30% effective
lessons.summary: From 1 April 2026 buybacks are capital gains again, with an extra charge for promoters.
lessons.title: Buyback tax: four regimes in thirteen years
lessons.plain: The tax on companies buying back their own shares has changed four times since 2013. From 1 April 2026, ordinary shareholders pay capital-gains tax only on their real profit. Promoters pay extra, for an effective 22% (companies) or 30% (individuals).

body: The General Anti-Avoidance Rule (Chapter X-A of the 1961 Act, carried into the 2025 Act) has applied since financial year 2017-18. It lets the tax department disregard an arrangement whose main purpose is a tax benefit and which lacks commercial substance, where the tax benefit in a year exceeds ₹3 crore.

For years, Azadi Bachao Andolan (2003) let investors rely on a Mauritius tax residency certificate. The 2016 protocols with Mauritius and Singapore made India the taxing country for gains on shares acquired from 1 April 2017, and grandfathered older holdings. In Tiger Global (15 January 2026) the Supreme Court held that grandfathering does not protect an impermissible avoidance arrangement and that GAAR can apply to a post-2017 exit from a pre-2017 investment.
Lawful planning now means substance: real decision-making, people and money where the entity claims to be resident, a commercial reason for each layer, and documents that show it.
keyPoints: GAAR since FY 2017-18; threshold ₹3 crore tax benefit
TRC necessary but not sufficient
Tiger Global (2026): grandfathering doesn’t shield avoidance
lessons.summary: A tax residency certificate is no longer a safe harbour.
lessons.title: Treaties, GAAR and the line between planning and avoidance
lessons.plain: Investors used to route money through countries like Mauritius to avoid Indian tax on their profits. Since 2017, India's anti-avoidance rule (GAAR) lets the tax department ignore structures that exist only to save tax. In the Tiger Global case (2026) the Supreme Court applied it. Today you need real business substance, not just paperwork.

body: In a flip, founders and investors hold shares in a Delaware or Singapore company, which owns the Indian company. The draw was investor familiarity (Delaware corporate law and its Court of Chancery, US-style SAFEs and preferred stock), dollar-denominated ESOPs, access to US listings, and for Singapore a strong treaty network and SIAC arbitration.

The costs are Indian ones. A foreign company whose place of effective management is in India is treated as Indian-resident for tax. Selling shares of the foreign company can be taxed in India as an indirect transfer when the shares derive substantial value from Indian assets (Indian assets above ₹10 crore and at least 50% of total assets). Transfer pricing applies between the holdco and the Indian company, and the 2022 overseas-investment rules govern how Indian residents hold the foreign shares.

US-only tax tools such as the section 83(b) election and the qualified small business stock exclusion help US taxpayers, not Indian-resident founders. Since 2022 the trend has reversed: see reverse flips.
keyPoints: Flip = foreign holdco above Indian opco
POEM in India makes the holdco Indian-resident
Indirect transfer tax applies when value comes from India
Tiger Global (2026) shows treaty routes may not protect the exit
lessons.summary: A ‘flip’ puts a foreign holding company on top of the Indian operating company.
lessons.title: Why startups flipped: Delaware, Singapore and the offshore holding company
lessons.plain: A 'flip' means putting a foreign company (often in Delaware or Singapore) on top of your Indian company, usually because foreign investors prefer it. It brings Indian tax risks. If the foreign company is really run from India, it can be taxed as Indian. Selling it can be taxed in India too. Many startups are now undoing flips.

body: The Foreign Exchange Management (Overseas Investment) Rules, Regulations and Directions, 2022 replaced the old ODI framework from 22 August 2022. Overseas direct investment can be made by cash or by a swap of shares, at arm’s-length value.

Round-tripping, once treated with suspicion, is now allowed with a structural cap: under Rule 19(3), an Indian resident cannot make a financial commitment in a foreign entity that has invested or invests into India if the result is a structure with more than two layers of subsidiaries.

Resident individuals face tighter limits than companies: they invest within the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (USD 250,000 a financial year) and only in operating foreign entities, not ones in financial services, with further conditions on controlling an entity that has its own subsidiaries. Check Schedule III of the OI Rules with counsel before any founder-level swap.
keyPoints: Share swaps are allowed ODI
Round-tripping allowed up to two layers of subsidiaries
Individuals: LRS USD 250,000 per year, operating entities only

sources.t: YourStory: flips under the new ODI framework

lessons.summary: Founders swapping Indian shares for foreign shares are making overseas direct investment.
lessons.title: Flip mechanics under the 2022 overseas-investment rules
lessons.plain: When Indian founders swap their Indian shares for shares in a foreign company, Indian rules treat that as investing abroad. Since 2022 this is allowed within limits: no more than two layers of subsidiaries when the money comes back into India. Individuals face extra limits, so check with a lawyer first.

body: The two routes are a share swap (investors swap foreign shares for Indian shares) and an inbound cross-border merger of the foreign parent into its Indian subsidiary under section 234 of the Companies Act and Rule 25A of the Compromises, Arrangements and Amalgamations Rules.

From 17 September 2024, Rule 25A(5) lets a foreign holding company merge into its wholly owned Indian subsidiary through the fast-track route in section 233 (Regional Director approval) instead of a full NCLT scheme; FEMA cross-border merger rules and RBI requirements still apply. MCA widened fast-track mergers again in September 2025.

The bill is tax. PhonePe’s investors paid about ₹8,000 crore in Indian tax when it moved from Singapore in 2022, as its CEO said publicly; Groww’s 2024 move from the US cost about USD 160 million in US tax according to reports. Plan the flip-back early: the cost grows with valuation.
keyPoints: Routes: share swap or inbound merger
Fast-track merger available for reverse flips since 17 Sep 2024
Exit tax arises where the gain is taxed: India, the US or elsewhere
lessons.summary: IPO plans in India have pulled PhonePe, Groww, Zepto, Razorpay, Pine Labs, Meesho and others back.
lessons.title: Reverse flipping: bringing the holding company home
lessons.plain: Startups planning to list in India are moving their parent company back home (a 'reverse flip'). It is done by swapping shares or merging the foreign parent into the Indian company, and since 2024 a faster merger route exists. The big cost is tax, which grows with the company's value. According to PhonePe's CEO, its investors paid about ₹8,000 crore.

body: Units in GIFT IFSC are regulated by the IFSCA and treated as non-residents for exchange-control purposes. Eligible IFSC units get a 100% income-tax deduction for 10 consecutive years out of 15, which is why fund managers and some fintech and aircraft-leasing businesses have set up there.

Indian public companies may list equity directly on IFSC exchanges under the permissible-jurisdiction listing framework introduced in 2024; MCA notified amendment rules to that framework on 3 November 2026, as reported.
For a startup, GIFT is mainly relevant for fund structures, treasury and fintech arms, not as a substitute holding company for the whole group.
keyPoints: IFSCA regulates; units treated as non-residents for FEMA
Tax holiday: 10 of 15 years
Direct listing route for public companies
lessons.summary: India’s International Financial Services Centre in Gujarat is the onshore alternative to Singapore.
lessons.title: GIFT IFSC: offshore treatment on Indian soil
lessons.plain: GIFT City in Gujarat is India's own 'offshore' financial zone. Businesses there are treated as foreign for currency rules, and eligible units get a 10-year tax break. It suits funds, treasury and fintech arms, not usually your whole company.

lessons.title: What a company is, and why founders form one
lessons.summary: A company is a separate legal 'person' that you own through shares.
lessons.plain: When you start a business properly, you create a company. The law treats it like a separate person: it signs contracts, owns things and owes money in its own name. If it fails, you normally lose only what you put in, not your house. That protection is why founders form companies.
body: Think of a company as a box the law treats as its own person. The box can sign contracts, open a bank account, hire people, own code and brands, borrow money, and sue or be sued, all in its own name. You, the founder, own the box through shares.

Because the company is separate, its debts are its own. If it fails, owners usually lose only the money they put in. This is called 'limited liability'. Exceptions exist: if you personally guarantee a loan or break the law, you can be on the hook.

In India most startups are private limited companies formed under the Companies Act, 2013 and registered with the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA). The company has directors (who run and oversee it) and shareholders (who own it). In a young startup, the founders are usually both.
keyPoints: A company is a separate legal person
Owners' risk is usually limited to what they put in
Directors run it; shareholders own it
Most Indian startups are private limited companies

lessons.title: Shares: who owns what
lessons.summary: Ownership is split into shares; your percentage is your shares divided by all shares.
lessons.plain: A company's ownership is cut into small pieces called shares. Your slice is simply your shares divided by all the shares. Owners vote on big decisions and share in the value when the company is sold. New shares for investors make everyone's slice smaller; that is called dilution.
body: Imagine the company as a pizza cut into slices. Each slice is a share. If there are 100 shares and you hold 60, you own 60%. The list of who holds what is the 'cap table'.

Owning shares usually gives you votes at shareholder meetings, a share of profits if the company pays dividends, and a share of the money if the company is sold. Different classes of shares can carry different rights. Investors often take 'preference shares' that are paid out first.

When the company sells new shares to raise money, the pizza gets more slices. You still hold the same number of shares, but your percentage drops. That is dilution. It is normal and fine if the company's value grows more than your slice shrinks. ESOPs and sweat equity also add slices.
keyPoints: Your % = your shares ÷ all shares
Shares bring votes and a claim on value
New shares dilute existing owners
Investors often get preference shares

lessons.title: How startups raise money
lessons.summary: Investors swap money for a slice of the company at an agreed valuation.
lessons.plain: Startups raise money in 'rounds'. An investor gives cash and gets new shares. How much they get depends on what the company is valued at. If someone puts in ₹1 crore at a ₹9 crore pre-money valuation, the company is worth ₹10 crore after, and they own 10%. Each round, you give up some ownership and often some control.
body: Money usually comes in stages. Early on: your own savings (bootstrapping), friends and family, and angel investors. Later: venture capital (VC) funds in rounds called Seed, Series A, Series B and so on.

The key number is the valuation, meaning what the company is agreed to be worth. 'Pre-money' is the value before the new money; 'post-money' is after. Investor's stake = their money ÷ post-money value. Example: ₹1 crore invested at ₹9 crore pre-money gives ₹10 crore post-money, so the investor owns 10%.

Investors don't only buy a percentage. They also ask for rights: board seats, vetoes over big decisions, and being paid first if the company is sold. These rights can matter more than the percentage, which is why the Founder Playbook volume focuses on them.
keyPoints: Rounds: angels → Seed → Series A, B…
Stake = investment ÷ post-money valuation
Investors also get rights, not just shares
Every round dilutes the founders

lessons.title: The papers founders sign
lessons.summary: Term sheet first, then the shareholders' agreement and changes to the articles.
lessons.plain: Raising money involves three key documents. The term sheet is a short summary of the deal. The shareholders' agreement (SHA) is the full contract between founders and investors. The articles of association are the company's official rulebook. In India, important rules must be in the articles too, or they may not bind everyone.
body: Term sheet: a few pages listing the main terms such as price, investor rights and conditions. It is mostly not binding, except usually exclusivity (you can't talk to other investors for a while) and confidentiality. Read it carefully: the final documents follow it.

Shareholders' agreement (SHA) and share subscription agreement (SSA): the full contracts. The SSA covers buying the new shares; the SHA covers how the company will be run afterwards: board seats, vetoes, rules on selling shares, and what happens on exit.

Articles of association: the company's own rulebook, filed with the MCA. Indian courts have held that share-transfer restrictions bind the company and shareholders only if they are in the articles. So investor rights from the SHA are copied into the articles after a round.
keyPoints: Term sheet = short, mostly non-binding summary
SHA = full founder–investor contract
Articles = company's official rulebook
Copy SHA rights into the articles

lessons.title: Who decides disputes
lessons.summary: Courts, the NCLT for company matters, and private arbitration.
lessons.plain: When people fight over a company, a few different bodies can decide. Normal courts handle most disputes, with the Supreme Court at the top. Company fights and insolvency go to a special tribunal called the NCLT. Many investment contracts instead choose arbitration, a private judge agreed in advance.
body: Courts: India has district courts, a High Court for each state (or group of states), and the Supreme Court at the top. Supreme Court rulings bind every court, and these rulings become precedents that later cases follow.

Tribunals: the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) hears company-law disputes, such as shareholders complaining of unfair treatment, and company insolvency cases. Appeals go to the NCLAT and then the Supreme Court.

Arbitration: parties can agree in their contract that disputes go to private arbitrators instead of court, often through an institution like SIAC in Singapore. The result, an 'award', can be enforced through the courts. It is usually faster and private, which is why investment contracts use it.
keyPoints: Supreme Court rulings bind all courts
NCLT: company disputes and insolvency
Arbitration: private, agreed in the contract
Awards are enforced through courts

lessons.title: Tax basics for founders
lessons.summary: Companies pay tax on profits; people pay tax on salary and on gains from selling shares.
lessons.plain: Tax shows up in three places for founders. The company pays income tax on its profits. You pay tax on your salary, and on any profit when you sell shares (capital gains). GST is a separate tax on sales. Since 1 April 2026, income tax is governed by the new Income-tax Act, 2025.
body: Company tax: a company pays income tax on its profits (income minus allowed costs). Startups that make losses pay little or none, and losses can often be carried forward to reduce tax in later profitable years.

Personal tax: as a founder or employee you pay tax on salary at slab rates. When you sell shares for more than you paid, the profit is a capital gain, taxed under separate rules that depend on how long you held them.

Other pieces: GST is a different tax charged on the sale of most goods and services. Tax treaties between countries decide which country taxes cross-border income. And anti-avoidance rules (GAAR) let the tax department ignore structures that exist only to save tax.
keyPoints: Company tax is on profits, not sales
Selling shares at a profit = capital gains
GST is separate from income tax
New Income-tax Act, 2025 since 1 April 2026

lessons.title: Foreign money and the RBI
lessons.summary: Money from abroad must follow FEMA rules on form, price and reporting.
lessons.plain: Money moving in and out of India is controlled by a law called FEMA, run by the RBI. When a foreign investor buys shares in your startup, the deal must use approved instruments, at a fair price, and be reported on time. Some investments need government approval first.
body: FEMA (the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999) controls cross-border money. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) administers it, and the government sets the foreign direct investment (FDI) policy, including which sectors are open.

Most sectors allow foreign investment under the 'automatic route' (no prior approval, just reporting afterwards). Some sectors, and investors linked to countries bordering India, need government approval first.

Foreign money must come in as instruments the rules treat as ownership (like shares or compulsorily convertible preference shares) at no less than a fair value, and must be reported to the RBI within deadlines. Going the other way, Indians investing abroad follow separate overseas-investment rules.
keyPoints: FEMA controls cross-border money; RBI runs it
Automatic route vs government approval
Right instrument, fair price, report on time
Investing abroad has its own rules

lessons.title: Go-to-market: who you sell to, where, and how
lessons.summary: A go-to-market (GTM) plan picks the first customer, the message, the channel, the sales motion and the price.
lessons.plain: Go-to-market means your plan for getting a product into customers' hands and getting paid. You decide who exactly you sell to first, why they should care, where they will find you, who does the selling (the product itself, a sales team or partners) and what you charge. Each of those choices also comes with legal rules, which the rest of Volumes VIII to XI cover.
body: A GTM plan answers five questions. (1) Ideal customer profile (ICP): the narrow group that feels the problem most and can pay. (2) Positioning: the one reason they should pick you over the alternative, including doing nothing. (3) Channels: where those customers already look, such as search, marketplaces, distributors, direct sales or communities. (4) Motion: product-led (users try and buy on their own), sales-led (people sell, usually to businesses) or partner-led (distributors, resellers, platforms). (5) Pricing and packaging.

Start with a beachhead: one segment you can win outright, then expand to the next. Track unit economics from day one: customer acquisition cost (CAC) against the gross margin a customer brings over their lifetime (LTV). If CAC is higher than LTV, growth only burns cash.

Legal checkpoints for each GTM choice: pricing and discounts (Competition Act, 2002, next lesson); dealers and distributors (rules on resale prices and exclusivity); marketplaces (Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 and FDI rules); ads and influencers (Volume X); consumer sales, refunds and contracts (Volume XI); your brand name and inventions (Volume IX). Build these into the plan before launch rather than after a notice arrives.
Use the Mood boards tab in the Playbook to set the look and feel of a launch, and check Volume IX before copying any brand's look too closely.
keyPoints: ICP → positioning → channel → motion → price
Win one beachhead segment first
Each GTM choice has a legal checklist (Vols VIII–XI)

lessons.title: Pricing, discounts and competition law
lessons.summary: Discounting is legal; controlling your dealers' resale prices, or pricing below cost while dominant, is not.
lessons.plain: You can set your own prices and run discounts. Two things get companies fined: telling independent dealers or resellers what price they must sell at (or how small a discount they may give), and, only if you dominate a market, selling below cost to push rivals out. Fines can reach 10% of turnover, and turnover now means global turnover.
body: The Competition Act, 2002 polices pricing in two ways. Section 3 bans anti-competitive agreements; section 3(4) covers vertical agreements along the supply chain (tie-ins, exclusive supply or distribution, refusal to deal and resale price maintenance) when they cause an appreciable adverse effect on competition in India. Section 4 bans abuse of a dominant position, including unfair or discriminatory prices and predatory pricing, meaning selling below cost to reduce competition or eliminate competitors.

Resale price maintenance in practice: on 23 August 2021 the CCI fined Maruti Suzuki ₹200 crore for a 'Discount Control Policy' that capped the discounts its dealers could give, enforced through mystery shopping agencies and penalties on dealers. Maruti's appeal is pending before NCLAT, which stayed the penalty in November 2021 on a 10% deposit. Recommending a price is generally safe; policing it is the risk.

Predatory pricing needs dominance first. A new startup giving launch discounts is rarely dominant, but platforms that become dominant face scrutiny of deep discounting, exclusivity and self-preferencing, as the CCI's Google Android case and its investigation of Amazon and Flipkart show.

Penalty: up to 10% of the average turnover of the last three financial years. Since the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023 and the CCI's penalty guidelines of 6 March 2024, 'turnover' for this purpose means global turnover.
keyPoints: Recommend prices to dealers; never enforce them
Below-cost pricing is illegal only for a dominant firm
Penalty up to 10% of average global turnover

sources.t: PIB: CCI penalty on Maruti, 23 Aug 2021
Business Standard: penalty on global turnover

lessons.title: Selling through marketplaces and your own online store
lessons.summary: The E-Commerce Rules set disclosure, grievance and cancellation duties; FDI rules keep foreign-funded marketplaces out of inventory.
lessons.plain: If you sell online, on Amazon or Flipkart or through your own site, the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 apply. Show who the seller is, the total price, return and refund terms and the country of origin, and have a grievance officer who answers complaints. If you run a marketplace with foreign investment, you may not own the stock sold on it.
body: The Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 were notified on 23 July 2020 and cover marketplace and inventory models, including platforms based abroad that systematically offer goods or services to people in India. A platform must appoint a grievance officer who acknowledges complaints within 48 hours and redresses them within one month; show the total price with a breakup of charges, seller details and country of origin; and must not charge cancellation fees unless it bears similar charges when it cancels an order itself.

FDI policy (Press Note 2 of 2018, in force from 1 February 2019) allows foreign investment only in the marketplace model. A foreign-funded marketplace cannot own or control the inventory sold on it; a seller in which the marketplace group holds equity cannot sell on that marketplace; and if more than 25% of a vendor's purchases come from the marketplace group, its inventory is treated as controlled by the marketplace.

A marketplace keeps 'intermediary' protection only while it stays passive. In Christian Louboutin v Nakul Bajaj (Delhi High Court, 2 November 2018) an online store that vouched for authenticity and ran the sale itself could not claim safe harbour for counterfeits. If you curate, warehouse or guarantee products, expect to carry the seller's legal risk.
keyPoints: Grievance officer: acknowledge in 48 hours
No one-sided cancellation fees
Foreign-funded marketplaces can't own inventory

lessons.title: The IP toolkit: trademarks, copyright, patents, designs, trade secrets
lessons.summary: Each right protects something different, lasts a different time and needs different paperwork.
lessons.plain: Intellectual property (IP) means owning what you create: your brand name and logo (trademark), your code, writing and artwork (copyright), a new technical invention (patent), the look of a product (design) and secret know-how (trade secret). Some rights arise automatically; others exist only after registration. Register the ones that matter before you launch publicly, and make sure the company, not individual people, owns them.
body: Trademark (Trade Marks Act, 1999): protects names, logos and slogans, and can cover the shape of goods, packaging or a combination of colours that identifies your business. Registration lasts 10 years and can be renewed again and again. Unregistered marks can still be protected through a 'passing off' action if you have built goodwill.

Copyright (Copyright Act, 1957): arises automatically for original code, text, art, music and film. For literary works, which include software, it lasts for the author's life plus 60 years. Registration is optional but is useful evidence. Copyright protects the expression, not the idea behind it.

Patent (Patents Act, 1970): a 20-year exclusive right over an invention that is new, inventive and capable of industrial use, granted only after examination. File before you disclose the invention publicly. Design (Designs Act, 2000): protects the visual shape, pattern or ornamentation of a product for 10 years, extendable by 5.

Trade secrets: India has no separate statute. Protection comes from contracts (NDAs, confidentiality and invention-assignment clauses) and the court action for breach of confidence. Every founder, employee and contractor should sign an IP assignment, or the company may not own what they build.

Startup benefits (SIPP scheme): DPIIT-recognised startups get an 80% rebate on patent filing fees, fast-tracked examination, and government-paid facilitator fees for patents, trademarks and designs; trademark filing fees for startups were cut by 50%.
keyPoints: Trademark 10 yrs (renewable) · Patent 20 yrs · Design 10+5
Copyright is automatic; registration is evidence
Get IP assignments from everyone who builds

lessons.title: Patents for software, AI and medicines
lessons.summary: Software 'per se' and minor drug tweaks are not inventions; a technical effect or real extra efficacy can be.
lessons.plain: India will not patent a computer program by itself, a business method or an algorithm. But software that produces a real technical result, such as faster or safer hardware, less memory, or a working device, can be patented. For medicines, a new form of a known drug is not patentable unless it works noticeably better as a treatment.
body: Section 3 of the Patents Act lists what is 'not an invention'. Section 3(k) excludes 'a mathematical or business method or a computer programme per se or algorithms'. Section 3(d) excludes new forms of a known substance unless they differ significantly in efficacy.

Software: in Ferid Allani v Union of India (Delhi High Court, 12 December 2019) the court said the bar applies to computer programs 'per se', not to every invention based on a program, and sent the application back to be examined for technical effect and technical contribution. The Patent Office's Guidelines for Examination of Computer Related Inventions, 2025 (released 29 July 2025) apply this approach and cover AI, machine-learning and blockchain inventions.

Medicines: in Novartis AG v Union of India (Supreme Court, 1 April 2013) the court refused a patent for the beta-crystalline form of imatinib (Glivec). Better bioavailability alone did not show enhanced therapeutic efficacy under section 3(d). This stops 'evergreening'.

Startup tactics: draft claims around the technical problem and the technical result, not the business outcome; keep lab notes and benchmark data that prove the effect; use the startup fee rebate and fast-tracked examination; and consider a provisional specification to secure your filing date, then file the complete specification within 12 months.
keyPoints: s.3(k): no patents for software 'per se'
Technical effect/contribution can make software patentable
s.3(d): a new form of a known drug needs better efficacy

sources.t: UNCTAD: Novartis v Union of India

lessons.title: Brand names and trademarks: choose a name you can own
lessons.summary: Invented names are strong, descriptive ones are weak, and earlier use can beat a later registration.
lessons.plain: A brand name is valuable only if you can stop others using it. Invented or unrelated words are easy to protect; names that simply describe the service ('BookMy…') are hard to protect. Search before you pick a name, file early, and remember that a business that used a name first can sometimes keep it even against a global brand.
body: Courts place marks on a spectrum: generic (never protectable), descriptive (protectable only after it gains a 'secondary meaning'), suggestive, and arbitrary or invented (strongest). In Bigtree Entertainment v Brain Seed Sportainment (Delhi High Court, 13 December 2017) BookMyShow could not stop 'bookmysports' because the prefix 'BOOKMY' described online booking and had not acquired distinctiveness.
Domain names are protected too. In Satyam Infoway v Sifynet Solutions (Supreme Court, 6 May 2004) the court held that domain names are protected like trademarks and that passing off applies to them.

Earlier use counts. Section 34 of the Trade Marks Act protects a person who has continuously used a mark from before the registered owner's use or registration, whichever is earlier. A Pune restaurant called Burger King since 1992 won at trial against Burger King Corporation in July 2024; the Bombay High Court restrained it on 2 December 2024; the Supreme Court stayed that order on 7 March 2025 and the appeal continues.

Search ads on a rival's name: in Google LLC v DRS Logistics (Delhi High Court, division bench, 10 August 2023) using a trademark as an ad keyword was 'use in advertising' but not infringement by itself; it infringes only if it causes confusion, takes unfair advantage or harms the mark. Google could not claim intermediary safe harbour for its Ads programme.

Colours and overall look: under section 2(1)(m) a 'mark' can include packaging or a combination of colours. Taking inspiration from a brand's mood is fine, but copying a famous brand's overall look in the same market invites a passing-off claim.
keyPoints: Invented > suggestive > descriptive > generic
Search, then file before launch
Earlier continuous use can defeat a later registration (s.34)

lessons.title: Ad claims and comparative advertising
lessons.summary: You may boast and compare honestly; you may not mislead or run down a rival's product.
lessons.plain: Ads can boast ('the best coffee in town') and can compare you with a rival, as long as the comparison is true and fair. You cannot make false or unproven claims, hide key conditions in tiny print, or unfairly make a rival look bad. The consumer regulator can fine advertisers and endorsers, and rivals can get court orders to pull the ad.
body: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 defines a 'misleading advertisement' in section 2(28). On 9 June 2022 the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) issued the Guidelines for Prevention of Misleading Advertisements and Endorsements for Misleading Advertisements, covering bait ads, 'free' claims, surrogate ads, ads aimed at children and endorsements. The CCPA can fine manufacturers, advertisers and endorsers up to ₹10 lakh, and up to ₹50 lakh for later contraventions, and can bar an endorser for up to 1 year, or 3 years for later contraventions.

Rivals enforce comparative-advertising limits in court. The principles from Reckitt & Colman v Kiwi TTK (Delhi High Court, 1996), Pepsi Co v Hindustan Coca Cola (Delhi High Court division bench, 2003) and Dabur India v Colortek Meghalaya (Delhi High Court division bench, 2 February 2010): puffery is allowed and you may say your product is the best or better, but you may not denigrate or defame a rival's goods. Courts look at the ad's intent, manner and overall message, and are stricter with TV because of its impact.

Same claim, different medium: Complan's 'one cup equals two cups of Horlicks' protein comparison survived as a print ad that explained the different serving sizes (Horlicks v Heinz, Delhi High Court, December 2018), but its TV commercial was restrained on 14 May 2020 (Horlicks v Zydus Wellness) because a few seconds on screen could not make the serving-size difference clear.
Working rules: hold substantiation (tests, data) before an ad runs; make disclaimers readable and in the same medium as the claim; compare like with like; never mock the rival's product.
keyPoints: Puffery yes, denigration no
Substantiate every factual claim before it airs
CCPA fines up to ₹10 lakh, ₹50 lakh for repeats; endorser bans

sources.t: Global Freedom of Expression: Horlicks v Heinz

lessons.title: Influencers, celebrities and the Patanjali rule
lessons.summary: Advertisers and endorsers share responsibility, and a self-declaration must be filed before an ad runs.
lessons.plain: If you pay influencers or celebrities to promote you, both you and they are answerable if the ad misleads. Paid posts must be clearly marked as ads. Since the Supreme Court's Patanjali order, advertisers must file a self-declaration that the ad follows the rules before it is published.
body: Indian Medical Association v Union of India (the Patanjali misleading-ads case): on 7 May 2024 the Supreme Court (Justices Hima Kohli and Ahsanuddin Amanullah) said advertisers and endorsers are responsible for misleading ads and that celebrities and influencers must act responsibly, and directed that a self-declaration be submitted before any advertisement is printed, aired or displayed, on the lines of Rule 7 of the Cable Television Networks Rules, 1994.

The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting put this into practice from June 2024: self-declaration certificates are required for ads across broadcast, print and digital media (TV and radio through the Broadcast Seva portal), and proof of upload is given to the broadcaster or publisher.

The CCPA's 2022 guidelines also cover endorsements: an endorsement should reflect the endorser's genuine opinion based on adequate information or experience, and any material connection with the brand, such as payment or a stake, must be disclosed. Since November 2023, 'disguised advertisement' (paid content made to look like organic content) is also a specified dark pattern.
Working rules: start paid posts with 'Ad' or 'Sponsored'; brief endorsers in writing with substantiated claims only; keep a copy of every self-declaration and every approved script.
keyPoints: Advertisers and endorsers are both answerable
Self-declare compliance before an ad runs
Label paid content clearly

lessons.title: Dark patterns, surrogate ads and 'T&C apply' tricks
lessons.summary: Thirteen dark patterns are specified, surrogate ads are prohibited, and a guarantee buried in fine print is misleading.
lessons.plain: Some growth tricks are now illegal in India: fake countdown timers, sneaking items into the cart, shaming people who say no, making cancellation hard, revealing extra fees only at checkout, and ads disguised as content. Advertising a banned product such as alcohol through a 'soda' or 'music' line with the same name is banned too. A big promise whose real conditions sit in tiny print counts as misleading.
body: On 30 November 2023 the CCPA notified the Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023, which list 13 specified dark patterns: false urgency, basket sneaking, confirm shaming, forced action, subscription trap, interface interference, bait and switch, drip pricing, disguised advertisement, nagging, trick question, SaaS billing and rogue malware. They apply to platforms systematically offering goods or services in India, and to advertisers and sellers.

Surrogate advertising: the 2022 misleading-ads guidelines prohibit surrogate or indirect ads for goods or services whose advertising is banned or restricted, for example promoting a liquor brand through a soda or music line carrying the same name.

Fine print is no defence. In August 2025 the CCPA fined Rapido ₹10 lakh over 'Guaranteed Auto' and 'Auto in 5 min or get ₹50' ads: the ₹50 was paid as Rapido coins usable only for bike rides and valid for 7 days, the 'T&C apply' text was too small to read, and the terms said the guarantee came from individual drivers rather than Rapido. It ordered the ads stopped and consumers compensated.
Audit your funnel: real stock and real deadlines only; add-ons only when the customer opts in; cancelling as easy as signing up; the full price shown up front; sponsored content labelled.
keyPoints: 13 specified dark patterns since 30 Nov 2023
Surrogate ads prohibited (2022 guidelines)
A headline promise must survive its own fine print

lessons.title: Selling to consumers: the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
lessons.summary: Consumers can complain cheaply to consumer commissions; one-sided terms and defective products carry real liability.
lessons.plain: Anyone who buys from you for personal use is a 'consumer' and can complain to a consumer commission cheaply, even without a lawyer. One-sided contract terms can be struck down, you are liable if your product is defective, and an arbitration clause will not keep a consumer out of the consumer commission.
body: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 has three tiers of consumer commissions. Under rules notified on 30 December 2021, District Commissions hear complaints where the price paid is up to ₹50 lakh, State Commissions above ₹50 lakh and up to ₹2 crore, and the National Commission above ₹2 crore. Complaints can be filed online through e-Daakhil.

Unfair contracts: section 2(46) defines an 'unfair contract', for example one requiring manifestly excessive security deposits, imposing disproportionate penalties, refusing early repayment, allowing one side to terminate without reasonable cause, or imposing other unreasonable conditions. The State and National Commissions can declare such terms null and void. Even under the 1986 Act, the Supreme Court in Pioneer Urban Land v Govindan Raghavan (2 April 2019) held that one-sided builder–buyer clauses were an unfair trade practice that did not bind the buyer.

Arbitration does not oust consumer commissions: in Emaar MGF Land v Aftab Singh (Supreme Court, review decided 10 December 2018) a consumer could pursue a consumer complaint despite an arbitration clause in the purchase agreement.

Product liability (Chapter VI of the 2019 Act) can make the manufacturer, the service provider and the seller of a product liable for harm caused by a defective product or deficient service, each on the grounds the Act lists. Keep warnings, instructions and quality records.
keyPoints: District ≤ ₹50 lakh · State ≤ ₹2 crore · National > ₹2 crore
One-sided terms can be declared void
An arbitration clause won't stop a consumer complaint
