lessons.title: B2B sales contracts that get you paid
lessons.summary: Clear scope, payment terms, a liability cap and the MSME 45-day rule protect your cash.
lessons.plain: When you sell to other businesses, the contract decides whether you get paid and how much you risk. Define what you deliver, when you get paid and what happens if you aren't, cap your liability, and use the MSME law: if you are a registered micro or small enterprise, buyers must pay you within 45 days or owe heavy interest.
body: Core clauses: scope and acceptance criteria; price, invoicing and payment period; interest on late payment; limitation of liability (usually a cap tied to fees paid, plus exclusion of indirect losses); indemnities limited to things you control, such as IP infringement; termination; and dispute resolution (governing law and seat of arbitration).

Damages: under sections 73 and 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 you recover losses that naturally arise from a breach. An agreed amount ('liquidated damages') works as a ceiling: courts award reasonable compensation up to that figure rather than paying it automatically.

MSME payments: under section 15 of the MSMED Act, 2006 a buyer must pay a micro or small enterprise supplier by the date agreed in writing, which can never be more than 45 days from acceptance; with no agreement, payment is due within 15 days. Late payment carries compound interest at three times the bank rate notified by the RBI (section 16), and the supplier can approach the Micro and Small Enterprises Facilitation Council (section 18).
Sales hygiene: make purchase orders incorporate your terms; record acceptance of deliveries; invoice promptly; for large or new accounts, ask for milestone or advance payments.
keyPoints: Cap liability; exclude indirect losses
Liquidated damages are a ceiling, not automatic
MSME suppliers must be paid within 45 days

lessons.title: Prices, MRP, refunds and warranties
lessons.summary: Show the full price, never charge above MRP on packaged goods, and honour your refund and warranty promises.
lessons.plain: Packaged goods must carry a maximum retail price (MRP) that includes all taxes, and you cannot charge more than it. Online, show the total price including all charges before checkout. Publish your return, refund and warranty terms and follow them, because breaking your own promises gives customers a consumer complaint.
body: The Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011 require pre-packaged goods to declare the retail sale price as a maximum retail price inclusive of all taxes, along with the maker's or packer's details, net quantity and a consumer-care contact. Online listings must show these declarations too. Selling above the MRP is an offence.
Drip pricing, revealing extra charges only at checkout, is a specified dark pattern since 30 November 2023, and the E-Commerce Rules require the total price with a breakup of charges.
Refunds and cancellations: platforms must display return, refund, exchange, warranty and delivery terms, and cannot charge cancellation fees unless they bear similar charges when they cancel.

Warranties are promises. Failing to honour one, or selling defective goods, exposes you to consumer complaints and product-liability claims. Write warranty terms in plain language, say clearly what is excluded, and keep service records.
keyPoints: MRP includes all taxes; never exceed it
Show the total price up front
Publish and honour return and refund terms

cases.facts: Amazon, an investor in a Future group company, objected to Future Retail’s asset sale to Reliance and obtained an emergency arbitrator’s order under SIAC rules in an India-seated arbitration.
cases.held: An emergency arbitrator’s order is an order under section 17(1) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act and is enforceable under section 17(2).
cases.name: Amazon.com NV Investment Holdings LLC v Future Retail Ltd
cases.why: Investors can get fast interim relief to block transactions that breach their protective rights. Founders should take negative covenants and consent rights seriously.

cases.facts: A CBDT circular said a Mauritius tax residency certificate was sufficient evidence of residence and beneficial ownership for treaty benefits. It was challenged as encouraging treaty shopping.
cases.held: The circular was valid. Treaty shopping was not illegal in itself, and the tax department could not deny treaty benefits by looking behind a valid residency certificate.
cases.name: Union of India v Azadi Bachao Andolan
cases.why: This made Mauritius the main route for foreign capital into Indian startups for over a decade. The 2016 protocol, GAAR from 2017 and Tiger Global (2026) have sharply limited it.

cases.facts: Biocon claimed the discount on shares issued to employees under its ESOP as a business expense; the tax department disallowed it as notional.
cases.held: The ESOP discount is employee compensation and an allowable business deduction, upholding a 2013 Special Bench ruling of the Bangalore ITAT.
cases.name: CIT v Biocon Ltd
cases.why: Startups can deduct ESOP cost when computing taxable profit.

cases.facts: The question was whether a company that did not sign an arbitration agreement could be bound by it because it belonged to the same group as a signatory.
cases.held: The group-of-companies doctrine is part of Indian arbitration law. A non-signatory can be bound where the parties’ conduct and the circumstances show a mutual intention that it be a party.
cases.name: Cox and Kings Ltd v SAP India Pvt Ltd
cases.why: Founders’ holding companies, a startup’s subsidiaries or an investor’s affiliates may be dragged into arbitration if they took part in the deal.

cases.facts: Indian distributors and end users paid foreign vendors for software licences. The tax department said the payments were royalties, so tax had to be withheld under section 195.
cases.held: Payments for end-user licences or resale of copies of software were not royalties under India’s tax treaties, because no copyright was transferred. No withholding was required.
cases.name: Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence Pvt Ltd v CIT
cases.why: Indian startups paying foreign SaaS and software vendors, and foreign SaaS companies selling into India, rely on this ruling to avoid treaty royalty withholding.

cases.facts: Formula One’s UK company licensed race-hosting rights to an Indian promoter and kept full control of the Buddh International Circuit around each Indian Grand Prix, an event lasting only a few days a year.
cases.held: The circuit was a fixed place of business at the foreign company’s disposal, so it had a permanent establishment in India and the income was taxable here.
cases.name: Formula One World Championship Ltd v CIT (International Taxation)
cases.why: A foreign holding company that runs real activity in India through a place it controls can have an Indian PE. Keep decision-making and operations consistent with the structure on paper.

cases.facts: An employee bound to work exclusively for the company for a fixed term left early to join a competitor.
cases.held: A negative covenant operating during the term of employment is not a restraint of trade under section 27 and can be enforced by injunction if reasonable.
cases.name: Niranjan Shankar Golikari v Century Spinning & Mfg Co Ltd
cases.why: Exclusivity while a founder or employee is still engaged is enforceable; the problem is only post-exit restraints.

cases.facts: A five-judge bench in N.N. Global (April 2023) had held that an unstamped agreement containing an arbitration clause was not enforceable at the appointment stage.
cases.held: Unstamped or insufficiently stamped agreements are inadmissible in evidence until duty is paid, but they are not void, and the defect is curable. At the appointment stage courts only check whether an arbitration agreement prima facie exists. N.N. Global was overruled.
cases.name: In re: Interplay between Arbitration Agreements under the Arbitration Act, 1996 and the Indian Stamp Act, 1899
cases.why: A stamping slip in an SHA or SSA will not kill the arbitration clause, but pay the duty: inadmissibility still bites in evidence.

cases.facts: A luxury brand sued an e-commerce site selling products under its marks, which claimed intermediary safe harbour.
cases.held: A platform that actively curates, stores, promotes and sells goods goes beyond a passive intermediary and may lose section 79 protection.
cases.name: Christian Louboutin SAS v Nakul Bajaj
cases.why: Marketplace startups that control inventory and listings carry more liability for counterfeit or infringing goods.

cases.facts: A distiller arranged for buyers to pay excise duty directly to the government so it would be left out of the turnover taxed as sales.
cases.held: Colourable devices cannot be part of tax planning, and arrangements made to dodge tax by dubious methods will not be respected.
cases.name: McDowell & Co. Ltd v Commercial Tax Officer
cases.why: Later benches (Azadi Bachao, Vodafone) confined it, saying genuine tax planning within the law is legitimate. Its spirit returned in statutory form through GAAR.

cases.facts: Shareholders had agreed between themselves on rights over their shares that were not reflected in the articles.
cases.held: A consensual arrangement between specific shareholders about their own shares can be enforced between them even though it is not in the articles, distinguishing V.B. Rangaraj.
cases.name: Messer Holdings Ltd v Shyam Madanmohan Ruia
cases.why: Gives some comfort that SHA terms bind the parties who signed, but the safer course remains to mirror them in the articles.

cases.facts: Investors bought a majority stake in Financial Software and Systems under a 2014 share acquisition and shareholders’ agreement governed by Indian law, with SIAC arbitration seated in Singapore. When the promised exit did not happen, a tribunal ruled for the investors. The Madras High Court enforced the award and the promoters appealed.
cases.held: The Supreme Court upheld enforcement, refused a disguised review of the tribunal’s reading of the shareholders’ agreement, applied the narrow public-policy test from Vijay Karia, and recognised transnational issue estoppel where the seat court had already rejected the same objections.
cases.name: Nagaraj V. Mylandla v PI Opportunities Fund-I
cases.why: Exit and put obligations promised to investors in an SHA will be enforced in India through foreign awards. Founders should negotiate exit clauses as if they will be enforced, because they will.

cases.facts: Foreign companies claimed lower withholding rates on dividends from India by invoking most-favoured-nation clauses in the protocols to India’s treaties with the Netherlands, France and Switzerland, pointing to later treaties India signed with countries that became OECD members afterwards.
cases.held: An MFN clause does not apply automatically; India must notify the benefit under section 90(1). The third country must also have been an OECD member when it signed its treaty with India.
cases.name: Assessing Officer (International Taxation) v Nestle SA
cases.why: Foreign investors in Indian startups cannot assume lower treaty rates through MFN clauses; withholding is at the notified treaty rate.

cases.facts: Two Indian companies agreed to arbitrate in Zurich. The losing party argued Indian parties could not opt out of Indian law by choosing a foreign seat.
cases.held: Two Indian parties may choose a foreign seat; this is not against public policy, and the award is enforceable in India as a foreign award under Part II.
cases.name: PASL Wind Solutions Pvt Ltd v GE Power Conversion India Pvt Ltd
cases.why: An Indian startup and its Indian investors can agree to Singapore or London arbitration.

cases.facts: A sports-management firm’s contract with cricketer Zaheer Khan gave it a right to match any offer he received after the contract ended.
cases.held: A negative covenant or right of first refusal operating after the contract ends is a restraint of trade and void under section 27 of the Indian Contract Act.
cases.name: Percept D’Mark (India) Pvt Ltd v Zaheer Khan
cases.why: Post-exit non-competes and matching rights over founders or employees are unenforceable in India.

cases.facts: Challenges to Aadhaar raised the question of whether the Constitution protects privacy.
cases.held: Privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21; restrictions must meet tests of legality, legitimate aim and proportionality.
cases.name: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India
cases.why: Led to the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, which every startup handling personal data must now comply with.

cases.facts: Family shareholders had agreed that shares could be transferred only within each branch of the family. The articles did not contain this restriction.
cases.held: A restriction on share transfers not contained in the articles of association binds neither the company nor the shareholders.
cases.name: V.B. Rangaraj v V.B. Gopalakrishnan
cases.why: Why every Indian term sheet requires the SHA’s transfer restrictions to be built into the articles.

cases.facts: Petitions challenged section 66A of the IT Act (criminalising ‘offensive’ online messages) and the intermediary takedown regime.
cases.held: Section 66A was struck down as unconstitutional. Under section 79, an intermediary loses protection only on actual knowledge through a court order or government notification.
cases.name: Shreya Singhal v Union of India
cases.why: The foundation of platform safe harbour for Indian marketplaces, social apps and SaaS products.

cases.facts: Cyrus Mistry was removed as executive chairman of Tata Sons. The NCLAT found oppression and ordered his reinstatement.
cases.held: Removal of a director or chairman is not by itself oppression or mismanagement; the NCLT cannot order reinstatement; affirmative voting rights in the articles were upheld.
cases.name: Tata Consultancy Services Ltd v Cyrus Investments Pvt Ltd
cases.why: A founder removed by the board cannot expect the NCLT to put them back. Protect founder board seats and roles expressly in the SHA and articles.

cases.facts: Three Mauritius entities of Tiger Global sold shares of Flipkart Singapore, which derived its value from Indian businesses, to Walmart’s Luxembourg vehicle in 2018 for about USD 1.6 billion. They claimed the gain was exempt under Article 13(4) of the India–Mauritius treaty and relied on valid tax residency certificates and grandfathering of pre-2017 investments. The Delhi High Court (2024) agreed with them.
cases.held: Reversing the High Court, the Supreme Court upheld the Authority for Advance Rulings: the structure was prima facie an impermissible tax-avoidance arrangement, GAAR could apply to a post-2017 exit even though the investment predated 2017, and a tax residency certificate does not conclusively establish treaty entitlement. The gains were taxable in India.
cases.name: Authority for Advance Rulings v Tiger Global International II Holdings
cases.why: Investors exiting Indian startups through Mauritius, Singapore or other treaty hubs must show commercial substance. Expect higher tax cost or litigation risk in exits, and price it into term sheets and secondary deals.

cases.facts: Indian shareholders of a joint venture resisted enforcement of a London award in favour of their Italian partner, arguing violations of natural justice and public policy.
cases.held: Grounds to resist a foreign award under section 48 are narrow; enforcement courts do not review merits, and the Supreme Court will interfere only in exceptional cases.
cases.name: Vijay Karia v Prysmian Cavi E Sistemi SRL
cases.why: Indian founders have little room to resist an adverse foreign award in a shareholder dispute.

cases.facts: Vodafone bought from Hutchison the shares of a Cayman Islands company that indirectly held Hutchison Essar’s Indian telecom business. The tax department said capital-gains tax should have been withheld because the value came from India.
cases.held: The transfer of shares of a foreign company between non-residents was not taxable in India under section 9 as then worded. Courts should ‘look at’ the whole transaction, not ‘look through’ genuine holding structures, and Vodafone had no withholding obligation.
cases.name: Vodafone International Holdings B.V. v Union of India
cases.why: Parliament reversed the result in 2012 by retrospectively taxing indirect transfers. Two international arbitral tribunals later ruled against India (Vodafone, Cairn), and the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021 withdrew retrospective demands for pre-May 2012 transfers. The prospective indirect-transfer rule still applies to flips.

cases.name: In re: Maruti Suzuki India Ltd (Discount Control Policy)
cases.facts: Acting on an anonymous email received in 2017, the CCI investigated Maruti's policy capping the discounts its dealers could give customers, enforced through mystery shopping agencies and penalties on dealers.
cases.held: The policy was resale price maintenance under section 3(4)(e) read with section 3(1) of the Competition Act, causing an appreciable adverse effect on competition. The CCI imposed a ₹200 crore penalty and a cease-and-desist order. NCLAT stayed the penalty on 22 November 2021 on a 10% deposit; the appeal is pending.
cases.why: Suggest retail prices to resellers if you like, but never police or punish their discounts.

src.t: PIB: CCI penalty on Maruti, 23 Aug 2021

cases.name: Google LLC v Competition Commission of India (Android)
cases.facts: In October 2022 the CCI fined Google ₹1,337.76 crore for abusing its dominant position in the Android mobile ecosystem through its agreements with device makers, and issued directions to change its conduct.
cases.held: NCLAT upheld the finding of abuse and the ₹1,337.76 crore penalty but set aside some of the CCI's directions. Google and the CCI have both appealed to the Supreme Court.
cases.why: Once a company is dominant, bundling and exclusivity terms that lock out rivals can cost a share of turnover. Startups competing with platforms can use competition law as a tool.

src.t: SCC Online: NCLAT on Google Android

cases.name: Amazon Seller Services v CCI; Flipkart Internet v CCI
cases.facts: On a complaint by Delhi Vyapar Mahasangh, a traders' body, the CCI ordered an investigation in January 2020 into exclusive phone launches, preferred sellers, deep discounting and preferential listing. Amazon and Flipkart challenged the order.
cases.held: The division bench refused to quash the probe, saying the companies should not hesitate to face an inquiry; the Supreme Court declined to interfere on 9 August 2021. Further challenges were later transferred to the Karnataka High Court.
cases.why: Marketplace design choices (who is promoted, exclusive launches, funded discounts) become competition-law questions once a platform is large.

src.t: LiveLaw: Karnataka HC on Amazon/Flipkart probe

cases.name: Novartis AG v Union of India
cases.facts: Novartis sought a patent for the beta-crystalline form of imatinib mesylate, sold as Glivec. The Patent Office rejected the application in 2006 and the IPAB upheld the rejection under section 3(d).
cases.held: A new form of a known substance is not an invention unless it shows significantly enhanced efficacy, which for a medicine means therapeutic efficacy. Improved bioavailability alone was not enough, so the rejection stood.
cases.why: Patent real improvements in outcome and keep the data that proves them; incremental tweaks will not extend a monopoly in India.

src.t: UNCTAD: Novartis v Union of India

cases.name: Ferid Allani v Union of India
cases.facts: Allani's 2002 application for a method and device for accessing information sources and services on the web was refused under section 3(k); the IPAB dismissed his appeal for lack of technical effect or advancement.
cases.held: The bar is on computer programs 'per se', not on all inventions based on computer programs. The court directed the Patent Office to re-examine the application in light of later guidelines and the technical-effect and technical-contribution test.
cases.why: Software-led startups can patent inventions that deliver a technical result; describe the technical contribution, not the business idea.

cases.name: Eastern Book Company v D.B. Modak
cases.facts: The publisher of the SCC law reports sued makers of legal software who copied its copy-edited versions of Supreme Court judgments.
cases.held: Labour alone ('sweat of the brow') does not create copyright; a derivative work needs some skill and judgment with a minimal degree of creativity. The judgment text itself stayed free to copy, while certain original editorial inputs were protected.
cases.why: Compiling public data is not automatically protected. Protect datasets and content through original selection and presentation, contracts and technical access controls.

src.t: Indian Kanoon: EBC v D.B. Modak

cases.name: Satyam Infoway Ltd v Sifynet Solutions Pvt Ltd
cases.facts: Satyam Infoway, which used 'Sify' as its trade name and in its domain names, objected to Sifynet Solutions using 'siffynet' domain names for its internet business.
cases.held: Domain names function as business identifiers and are protected like trademarks; passing off applies to them. The Supreme Court restored the injunction in favour of Satyam Infoway.
cases.why: Secure the domain and trademark together, and act quickly against look-alike domains.

cases.name: Bigtree Entertainment Pvt Ltd v Brain Seed Sportainment Pvt Ltd
cases.facts: BookMyShow's owner sought to stop a sports-facility booking platform using 'bookmysports' and the 'BOOKMY' prefix.
cases.held: No interim injunction: 'BOOKMY' is descriptive of online booking, other websites used it, and there was no evidence that it had acquired distinctiveness linked only to BookMyShow.
cases.why: Descriptive names are cheap to adopt and expensive to defend. Pick a distinctive brand you can actually stop others from using.

cases.name: Burger King Corporation v Anahita Irani
cases.court: Pune District Court; Bombay High Court; Supreme Court
cases.facts: In 2011 Burger King Corporation sued the Iranis, whose Pune restaurant has traded as Burger King since 1992, for trademark infringement and passing off.
cases.held: The Pune court dismissed the suit in July 2024, relying on the restaurant's prior use. The Bombay High Court restrained the restaurant on 2 December 2024 pending appeal; the Supreme Court stayed that order on 7 March 2025 and asked the High Court to decide the appeal quickly. The final outcome is awaited.
cases.why: A registration does not automatically beat a local business's earlier continuous use (section 34). Big brands should register and enforce early; small brands should keep proof of first use.

src.t: Business Standard: SC stays Bombay HC order

cases.name: Google LLC v DRS Logistics (P) Ltd
cases.facts: Agarwal Packers and Movers objected to rivals bidding on its trademark as keywords in Google Ads.
cases.held: Using a trademark as a keyword to trigger ads is 'use in advertising' under section 29(6), but is not infringement by itself; it infringes only with confusion, unfair advantage, dilution or harm to the mark. Google is not entitled to intermediary safe harbour for its Ads programme.
cases.why: You may bid on category words; bidding on a rival's brand is risky if the ad could confuse, and never put their mark in your ad text.

src.t: SCC Online: Google v DRS Logistics

cases.name: Pepsi Co Inc v Hindustan Coca Cola Ltd
cases.facts: Pepsi sued over Coca-Cola's commercials for its Thums Up drink, which it said ridiculed Pepsi.
cases.held: To decide disparagement a court looks at the intent of the commercial, its manner and storyline, and the overall message. Viewing the ad as a whole, the division bench held that it disparaged the rival's product.
cases.why: Comparisons are allowed; mocking the rival's product is not. Courts judge the whole ad, not just the words.

src.t: Indian Kanoon: Pepsi v Coca-Cola applied

cases.name: Dabur India Ltd v Colortek Meghalaya Pvt Ltd
cases.facts: In a dispute between two makers of mosquito-repellent creams, Dabur said Colortek's TV commercial disparaged its product.
cases.held: Ads are commercial speech protected by Article 19(1)(a) but must not be false, misleading, unfair or deceptive. Hyper-sensitivity is unwarranted; only untruthful disparagement is actionable. The bench upheld the finding that this ad did not disparage Dabur.
cases.why: Know the line: exaggerated self-praise is fine, false or misleading statements about the rival are not.

cases.name: Horlicks Ltd v Zydus Wellness Products Ltd
cases.facts: Zydus's TV commercial claimed one cup of Complan had as much protein as two cups of Horlicks, based on different recommended serving sizes.
cases.held: Interim injunction granted: the TV ad was prima facie misleading and disparaging because viewers could not take in the serving-size difference in a short commercial. A similar print comparison with the explanation had survived in 2018.
cases.why: A comparison that needs a footnote may work in print but fail on TV or in short video. Match the disclosure to the medium.

cases.name: Indian Medical Association v Union of India (Patanjali)
cases.facts: The IMA petitioned against Patanjali's misleading advertisements about modern medicine and its products, and sought wider regulation of misleading ads.
cases.held: Advertisers and endorsers are responsible for misleading ads; celebrities and influencers must act responsibly. Before an ad is printed, aired or displayed, a self-declaration must be submitted on the lines of Rule 7 of the Cable Television Networks Rules, 1994.
cases.why: Build a pre-publication compliance step into every campaign and keep the self-declarations on file.

src.t: LiveLaw: SC directions on misleading ads

cases.name: In re: Roppen Transportation Services (Rapido)
cases.facts: Rapido advertised 'Guaranteed Auto' and 'Auto in 5 min or get ₹50'. The ₹50 was given as Rapido coins for bike rides only, valid for 7 days, the T&C text was unreadably small, and the terms said individual drivers gave the guarantee.
cases.held: Misleading advertisement and unfair trade practice: penalty of ₹10 lakh, the ads to be discontinued, and consumers who did not get the promised ₹50 to be compensated in full.
cases.why: A guarantee must be honoured on its plain meaning. If the conditions change the deal, they belong in the headline.

cases.name: Emaar MGF Land Ltd v Aftab Singh
cases.facts: A villa buyer filed a consumer complaint over delayed possession. The builder relied on the arbitration clause in the buyer's agreement and the amended section 8 of the Arbitration Act.
cases.held: Consumer disputes can be pursued before consumer forums despite an arbitration agreement; the amended section 8 does not take away the consumer's statutory remedy. The review petition was dismissed.
cases.why: An arbitration clause in consumer terms will not keep customers out of consumer commissions. Budget for consumer complaints and resolve them early.

src.t: Supreme Court: Emaar MGF v Aftab Singh

cases.name: Pioneer Urban Land & Infrastructure Ltd v Govindan Raghavan
cases.facts: A flat buyer sought a refund after long delays. The builder's agreement gave it wide rights and heavy forfeiture while capping its own liability for delay.
cases.held: Buyers had no real choice but to sign on the dotted line; ex-facie one-sided, unfair and unreasonable terms are an unfair trade practice and do not bind the buyer. The builder had to refund with interest.
cases.why: Write customer terms that are balanced and defensible; one-sided clauses may simply be ignored by the court.

gaps.closed: The labour codes (21 November 2025) define ‘wages’ uniformly; allowances above 50% of total remuneration are added back to wages.
gaps.gap: Provident fund and gratuity were calculated on basic pay, so employers kept basic low and paid the rest as allowances.
gaps.title: Keeping basic pay low to cut PF and gratuity
gaps.today: Design CTC so that wages are at least half of total pay; budget for higher PF and gratuity.
gaps.used: Common in startup salary structures to reduce employer contributions and increase take-home pay.

gaps.closed: Finance Act 2012 taxed premium above fair value as the company’s income (s.56(2)(viib)). DPIIT exemptions followed in 2019; Finance Act 2023 extended the tax to non-resident investors. Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 abolished it from assessment year 2025-26 (shares issued from FY 2024-25). The Income-tax Act, 2025 has no equivalent.
gaps.gap: Unaccounted money could be brought into a closely held company as a high share premium from friendly investors.
gaps.title: Share premium and the angel tax
gaps.today: Valuation still matters: FEMA pricing for foreign investors, Companies Act valuer reports, and reassessments of rounds raised before FY 2024-25.
gaps.used: Shell companies issued shares at inflated premiums to launder cash; genuine startups raising at high valuations were caught by the anti-abuse rule meant for them.

gaps.closed: A 20% company-level buyback tax for unlisted companies (2013), extended to listed companies (2019); then from 1 October 2024 buybacks were taxed as dividends in shareholders’ hands. From 1 April 2026 they are capital gains again, but promoters pay an additional tax for an effective 22% (corporate) or 30% (non-corporate).
gaps.gap: Buyback proceeds were taxed as capital gains while dividends carried dividend distribution tax, so returning cash by buyback was cheaper.
gaps.title: Buybacks instead of dividends
gaps.today: Buybacks are an efficient liquidity tool for employees and small investors; for promoters the effective rate is fixed by the add-on.
gaps.used: Unlisted and later listed companies distributed profits to promoters through buybacks.

gaps.closed: Finance Act 2012 retrospectively taxed indirect transfers where foreign shares derive substantial value from Indian assets. After arbitral tribunals ruled against India in the Vodafone and Cairn treaty cases (2020), the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021 dropped retrospective demands for transfers before 28 May 2012 but kept the rule for later transfers.
gaps.gap: Before 2012, selling shares of a foreign company that owned Indian businesses was outside Indian tax, even though all the value came from India.

timeline.e: Vodafone buys Hutchison’s Indian business via a Cayman company
Supreme Court rules for Vodafone; Parliament amends the law retrospectively
Vodafone and Cairn win treaty arbitrations
Retrospective demands withdrawn; prospective rule stays

gaps.title: Selling the offshore parent instead of the Indian company
gaps.today: Indirect transfers are taxable where Indian assets exceed ₹10 crore and make up at least 50% of the foreign company’s value; small shareholders without control have an exemption.
gaps.used: Exits and acquisitions were done at the offshore holding-company level (Vodafone–Hutchison being the best-known example).

gaps.closed: Section 79 (now s.119 of the 2025 Act) cancels carried-forward losses of closely held companies when 51% voting continuity breaks. Eligible startups get an alternative test: losses survive if all loss-year shareholders keep their shares.
gaps.gap: Tax losses could be used by whoever bought the company.

timeline.e: Startup relief window extended to 10 years from incorporation
Carried into s.119 of the 2025 Act

gaps.title: Buying a loss-making company to use its losses
gaps.today: Genuine startups can keep losses through dilutive rounds; secondaries that fully exit an original shareholder can still forfeit them.
gaps.used: Acquirers bought loss-making shells to set the losses off against new profits.

gaps.closed: 2016 protocols gave India the right to tax gains on shares acquired from 1 April 2017, grandfathering earlier holdings. GAAR took effect the same year. In Tiger Global (Jan 2026) the Supreme Court held that grandfathering and a TRC do not protect an arrangement lacking commercial substance.
gaps.gap: Under the old India–Mauritius and India–Singapore treaties, capital gains on Indian shares were taxable only in the investor’s country of residence, which did not tax them.

timeline.e: CBDT Circular 789: a Mauritius TRC is enough
Azadi Bachao Andolan upholds the circular
Source taxation for new investments; GAAR in force
Tiger Global: GAAR applied to a grandfathered investment’s exit

gaps.title: Mauritius and Singapore treaty route for capital gains
gaps.today: Treaty benefits remain available to entities with real substance and commercial purpose. Plan for Indian capital-gains tax on exits unless the structure can withstand GAAR.
gaps.used: Foreign funds invested in Indian startups through Mauritius or Singapore companies holding a tax residency certificate, so exits paid no capital-gains tax anywhere.

gaps.closed: In Nestle SA (2023) the Supreme Court required a government notification under section 90(1) and OECD membership at the time of the other treaty.
gaps.gap: Protocols to some treaties promised to extend lower rates India later gave OECD countries, and taxpayers argued this applied automatically.

timeline.e: Delhi High Court allows MFN benefit

gaps.title: Importing lower treaty rates through MFN clauses
gaps.today: Use the rate in the notified treaty text; do not rely on MFN without a notification.
gaps.used: Foreign shareholders claimed 5% dividend withholding instead of 10%, citing treaties India signed with countries that later joined the OECD.

gaps.closed: The 2022 overseas-investment rules permit such structures but cap them at two layers of subsidiaries (Rule 19(3)). POEM rules, transfer pricing and GAAR address the tax side.
gaps.gap: Indian founders owning a foreign company that invests back into India can disguise domestic money as foreign investment or move profits offshore.

timeline.e: RBI treats round-tripping as suspect; approvals needed
OI Rules allow it within two layers

gaps.title: Round-tripping through offshore holding companies
gaps.today: A flip with genuine commercial reasons and at most two subsidiary layers is lawful; layering to hide ownership or shift profits is not.
gaps.used: Flip structures and earlier offshore layering, which the RBI restricted case by case before 2022.

gaps.title: Controlling inventory through 'independent' sellers on a foreign-funded marketplace
gaps.gap: FDI was allowed in the marketplace model but not in inventory-based e-commerce, yet nothing stopped a marketplace's own group from owning stakes in its biggest sellers.
gaps.used: Sellers linked to platform groups became top sellers, letting the marketplace influence stock and prices while claiming to be only a platform.
gaps.closed: Press Note 2 (2018), in force from 1 February 2019: a marketplace cannot own or control inventory; a vendor in which the marketplace group holds equity cannot sell on it; and if more than 25% of a vendor's purchases come from the group, its inventory counts as controlled by the marketplace.

timeline.e: Press Note 3 allows 100% FDI in the marketplace model only

gaps.today: If you raise foreign money for a marketplace, keep sellers genuinely independent, on arm's-length terms, and document it.

gaps.title: Extending drug patents with minor tweaks ('evergreening')
gaps.gap: Companies filed new patents on new salts, crystal forms or combinations of known drugs, extending exclusivity beyond the original 20 years.
gaps.used: A familiar strategy for blockbuster drugs in many countries.
gaps.closed: Section 3(d), added by the Patents (Amendment) Act, 2005, refuses new forms of known substances unless efficacy is significantly enhanced. The Supreme Court applied it in Novartis on 1 April 2013.
gaps.today: For pharma and chemistry startups: patent genuine therapeutic improvements and keep the efficacy data.

src.t: UNCTAD: Novartis v Union of India

gaps.title: Patenting software by proving a technical effect
gaps.gap: Section 3(k) bars computer programs 'per se', but the Act never defined 'per se'.
gaps.used: Applicants frame claims around the technical problem and technical result (hardware efficiency, security, signal processing) rather than the business logic.
gaps.closed: Not closed: the Delhi High Court endorsed the technical-effect test in Ferid Allani (2019), and the 2025 CRI Guidelines apply it. Pure business methods and algorithms remain excluded.
gaps.today: Lawful planning: describe and evidence the technical contribution; do not claim the business method itself.

gaps.title: Bidding on a rival's brand name as a search-ad keyword
gaps.gap: Search engines let any business show its ad when users search for a rival's brand name.
gaps.used: Rivals bought each other's brand names as keywords; MakeMyTrip, for example, sued over Booking.com's ads on 'MakeMyTrip'.
gaps.closed: Google v DRS Logistics (2023): keyword use is 'use in advertising' but not infringement by itself; it becomes infringement with confusion, unfair advantage or dilution. Google cannot rely on safe harbour for its Ads programme.
gaps.today: Bidding on a rival's name is risky if your ad could confuse; never use their mark in your ad text.

src.t: SCC Online: Google v DRS Logistics

gaps.title: Surrogate ads for liquor and tobacco brands
gaps.gap: Ads for liquor and tobacco are banned on TV, but the same brand name could be advertised on a soda, water or music product.
gaps.used: Brands kept their names on screen through 'brand extensions' that were rarely the real business.
gaps.closed: The CCPA's misleading-ads guidelines of 9 June 2022 prohibit surrogate or indirect ads for goods whose advertising is banned or restricted.
gaps.today: Promote a restricted product's brand only where the law allows; a token brand extension will not protect the campaign.

gaps.title: Paid promotions passed off as personal opinion
gaps.gap: Influencer and celebrity posts did not have to say they were paid.
gaps.used: Brands paid for 'honest reviews' and endorsements without disclosure, borrowing the endorser's credibility.
gaps.closed: The 2022 CCPA guidelines require endorsements to be genuine and material connections disclosed; disguised advertisement became a specified dark pattern on 30 November 2023; and on 7 May 2024 the Supreme Court held endorsers equally responsible for misleading ads.

timeline.e: Disguised ads listed as a dark pattern

gaps.today: Label every paid post and brief endorsers with substantiated claims only.

src.t: LiveLaw: SC directions on misleading ads

gaps.title: Big guarantees with the real conditions in fine print
gaps.gap: A headline promise could be qualified by small-print terms that changed what the customer actually got.
gaps.used: Delivery and ride-hailing apps advertised guarantees backed by restrictive credits or conditions.
gaps.closed: The CCPA treats such ads as misleading. In August 2025 it fined Rapido ₹10 lakh for its 'Auto in 5 min or get ₹50' campaign and ordered compensation.
gaps.today: If a condition changes the deal, put it in the headline, in readable type.

gaps.title: Using arbitration clauses to keep customers out of consumer courts
gaps.gap: Sellers inserted arbitration clauses into consumer contracts, and the 2015 change to section 8 of the Arbitration Act seemed to require courts to refer disputes to arbitration.
gaps.used: Builders and service providers relied on arbitration to make consumer complaints slower and costlier.
gaps.closed: Emaar MGF Land v Aftab Singh (Supreme Court, February and December 2018): consumers can still go to consumer forums despite an arbitration clause.

timeline.e: Section 8 of the Arbitration Act amended

gaps.today: Expect consumer complaints regardless of your dispute clause, and resolve them early.

src.t: Supreme Court: Emaar MGF v Aftab Singh

gaps.title: One-sided standard-form contracts
gaps.gap: Customers had to accept the seller's printed terms, which often had heavy forfeitures for the customer and tiny penalties for the seller.
gaps.used: Common in real estate, subscriptions and financial products.
gaps.closed: Pioneer Urban Land v Govindan Raghavan (Supreme Court, 2 April 2019) held such terms an unfair trade practice; the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 defines 'unfair contract' (section 2(46)) and lets State and National Commissions declare such terms void.

timeline.e: Supreme Court: one-sided terms don't bind

gaps.today: Draft balanced consumer terms; mirror any penalty you impose with one you accept.

src.t: Supreme Court: Pioneer v Govindan Raghavan

gaps.title: Revealing fees only at checkout ('drip pricing')
gaps.gap: A low headline price drew customers in, and convenience, platform or handling fees appeared only on the final screen.
gaps.used: Common in ticketing, travel, food delivery and quick commerce.
gaps.closed: The E-Commerce Rules, 2020 require the total price with a breakup of charges; drip pricing became a specified dark pattern on 30 November 2023.
gaps.today: Show the full price on the first screen where a price appears.

stories.apply: In an Indian private company you can copy the idea with a promoter holding company or trust holding differential-voting shares (within the 74% voting cap) and board-nomination rights in the articles. Decide this before your first priced round.
stories.lesson: A ‘golden share’ works best when its purpose is written down, it is held by someone other than the people it protects, and it has a defined end.
stories.move: Control was designed before outside capital dominated, with a stated purpose (the mission), independent trustees, and rules for how the structure itself can be amended. The founders hold a majority of shareholder votes, but the board majority sits with the Trust, so it constrains founders as well as investors.
stories.name: Anthropic: a mission trust plus founder supervoting
stories.what: Anthropic is a public benefit corporation. Since 2023 its Long-Term Benefit Trust, five financially disinterested trustees, has held Class T stock with power to elect a growing share of the board, reaching a majority. Reporting on the 26 October 2026 IPO filing says the Trust elects four of seven directors, while a Class F share held by the co-founders’ company carries 50.1% of the general vote and elects the other three; after Class F lapses the board becomes staggered.

stories.apply: Never hold shares informally on someone’s behalf; keep relatives out of vendor and payment flows; document every founder arrangement.
stories.lesson: A board can remove a founder-MD; an unclean cap table (shares held informally for others) multiplies the fights.
stories.move: Allegations about vendor payments and family involvement gave the board grounds to act, and informal share-holding arrangements between co-founders created separate lawsuits.
stories.name: BharatPe vs Ashneer Grover
stories.what: BharatPe’s board removed Grover as managing director in March 2022. In January 2023 the company sued him and family members in the Delhi High Court alleging embezzlement and seeking up to ₹88.67 crore. Co-founders separately sued to recover shares they said Grover held for them. In September 2024 the parties settled: Grover left the company and its shareholding, some of his shares went to a company trust and the rest to a family trust, and both sides dropped legal action.

stories.apply: Before any large loan, have counsel list the events of default and what lenders can seize; avoid personal acknowledgements and guarantees; keep loan proceeds in traceable, approved accounts; and comply with court orders while you contest them.
stories.lesson: Debt is control: covenants, events of default and governing law decide who runs the company when things go wrong. Ignoring a foreign court makes things worse.
stories.move: Borrowing heavily under US law with founder acknowledgements of default, then disputes with lenders and non-compliance with US court orders, moved control to creditors and courts in two countries.
stories.name: Byju’s: foreign-law debt, lenders and insolvency

src.t: Onmanorama: Kerala HC split verdict on stay (Oct 2026)
LiveLaw Biz: NCLT dismisses founders’ impleadment pleas (Nov 2026)

stories.status: Ongoing. On 29 Oct 2026 a Kerala High Court bench split over staying its June ruling in a creditor’s review petition, and the matter went to a third judge. On 18 Nov 2026, NCLT Bengaluru was reported to have dismissed the founders’ pleas to be made parties to the insolvency. US proceedings are still going.
stories.what: Byju’s raised a $1.2 billion US-law term loan through a US subsidiary, Byju’s Alpha. After default, the lenders’ agent GLAS Trust took control of Alpha, a right the Delaware Supreme Court upheld. Lenders allege $533 million of loan proceeds were moved out; in November 2025 a Delaware bankruptcy court entered a default judgment of over $1 billion against Raveendran for not complying with discovery, which it later reopened to determine damages. In India, insolvency proceedings started over dues to the BCCI; the Supreme Court set aside a settlement that would have ended them and in November 2025 declined to halt them. Raveendran denies wrongdoing and calls the lenders’ actions a ‘corporate raid’.

stories.apply: Put differential voting and board rights in the articles before investors join. Any later change that helps you should go through independent directors and a separate vote of the other shareholders.
stories.lesson: Control locked in at founding or IPO is defensible; changing the rules later in your own favour invites a lawsuit even if you win the vote.
stories.move: He tried to extend control after the IPO by changing the capital structure while already the controlling holder, which brought fiduciary-duty scrutiny.
stories.name: Facebook’s non-voting Class C plan
stories.what: Zuckerberg controlled about 60% of Facebook’s vote through Class B shares. In April 2016 Facebook announced a dividend of two non-voting Class C shares per existing share so he could sell stock for philanthropy without losing control. About 80% of minority shareholders voted against it, but his votes carried it. Shareholders sued in the Delaware Court of Chancery, and in September 2017, days before he was due to testify, Facebook withdrew the plan.

stories.apply: Make exit obligations the company’s, best-efforts, time-limited and at fair value; never personally guarantee an investor’s return.
stories.lesson: Exit and put obligations in an SHA will be enforced against founders, including through foreign arbitration.
stories.move: The promoters signed exit obligations they could not deliver and then tried to re-argue the contract in enforcement proceedings.
stories.name: Financial Software and Systems: the exit promise that was enforced
stories.what: Under a 2014 agreement, investors took a substantial stake and the promoters committed to provide an exit. When it did not happen, a SIAC tribunal in Singapore ruled for the investors. The Madras High Court enforced the award and on 25 March 2026 the Supreme Court refused the promoters’ challenge.

stories.apply: Report the same numbers to every investor, reconcile to audited accounts, and act on auditor red flags immediately.
stories.lesson: Inflated numbers are found at the next diligence, and the consequences become criminal, not just commercial.
stories.move: Growth-at-all-costs reporting that could not survive a professional audit.
stories.name: GoMechanic: misreporting found in diligence
stories.what: During diligence for a SoftBank-led round, EY found problems; in January 2023 the founders told investors of serious inaccuracies in financial reporting. The deal collapsed, about 70% of staff were laid off, and the business was sold to a consortium. Auditors had reportedly flagged accounting non-compliance in earlier years, and a later police FIR alleged funds were siphoned through a related entity.

stories.apply: Know exactly who can remove you under your documents, keep board relationships healthy, and do not assume founder status protects your role.
stories.lesson: Formal control and practical power can diverge. Boards can fire founders, but legitimacy with staff and investors decides whether it sticks.
stories.move: Altman did not control the board, but he had the support of employees and the largest investor, which made the board’s decision untenable.
stories.name: OpenAI: fired by the board, back in five days
stories.what: On 17 November 2023 OpenAI’s board removed CEO and co-founder Sam Altman, saying he had not been consistently candid. Around 97% of employees signed a letter demanding the board resign, and on 22 November he was reinstated with a new initial board chaired by Bret Taylor.

stories.apply: Have a co-founder agreement with vesting, leaver terms and pre-emption rights from day one, and get your own lawyer for any restructuring or flip.
stories.lesson: Every early document that moves shares into a new entity can decide your ownership. Read the share mechanics, vesting and issuance authority, not just the headline percentage.
stories.move: He signed restructuring documents without protecting his stake or understanding how new share issuances would dilute him.
stories.name: Eduardo Saverin’s dilution at Facebook
stories.what: During Facebook’s 2004–05 restructuring into a new corporation, co-founder Eduardo Saverin’s stake was heavily diluted and he was sidelined. He sued, claiming he had been fraudulently induced to sign the agreement setting his share interest; Facebook countersued. The dispute ended in a confidential settlement.

stories.apply: Have your own pay, loans and related-party deals approved by directors and shareholders who are independent of you, with written reasons.
stories.lesson: When a powerful founder benefits from a board decision, the process (independent directors, full disclosure, approval by other shareholders) is what protects it.
stories.move: The deal survived on appeal, but only after seven years of litigation over whether the board was independent of Musk.
stories.name: Tesla: the founder pay package that went to court
stories.what: A shareholder holding nine Tesla shares challenged Musk’s 2018 package, then worth about $56 billion. In 2024 the Delaware Court of Chancery found Musk was a controlling stockholder, held the process unfair and rescinded the package. On 19 December 2025 the Delaware Supreme Court reversed the rescission, awarded nominal damages of $1 and cut the plaintiff’s fee award. Tesla had meanwhile reincorporated in Texas.

stories.apply: Tie your board seats to clear thresholds in the articles, disclose fully when asking for new rights, and keep an arbitration clause in founder agreements so disputes stay private.
stories.lesson: Board appointment rights are the real battleground. A founder can keep shares and still lose the CEO job.
stories.move: The fight centred on who could appoint directors. Kalanick held seat-appointment rights; investors attacked how he obtained them.
stories.name: Uber: Kalanick, Benchmark and the board-seat fight
stories.what: Kalanick resigned as Uber CEO in June 2017 under investor pressure after an investigation into the company’s culture. In August 2017 Benchmark, holding about 13%, sued in Delaware to remove him from the board, alleging he had misled directors into giving him power to fill three extra board seats. The court sent the case to arbitration and Benchmark dropped it in January 2018 as a condition of SoftBank’s investment.

stories.apply: Keep related-party dealings minimal and documented, and keep the business fundable on its numbers; that, not voting shares, is the real protection.
stories.lesson: Control rights are only as strong as your ability to raise the next round. Investors with the money can force change regardless of voting rights.
stories.move: Extreme founder control combined with self-interested arrangements and losses made the company unsellable to public investors.
stories.name: WeWork: supervoting shares couldn’t save the founder
stories.what: WeWork’s 2019 IPO prospectus showed heavy losses and governance concerns, including Neumann borrowing against his shares and seeking 20 votes per share. Investors pushed back, he resigned as CEO in September 2019, the IPO was withdrawn, and SoftBank paid him about $1.7 billion to step back. WeWork later listed via a SPAC and filed for Chapter 11 in November 2023.

stories.apply: For each new venture, ask whether it can reach profitability on founder or customer money before taking VC; raise only when capital clearly buys growth you cannot otherwise get.
stories.lesson: The strongest founder protection is not needing the money. Every round trades some control for capital.
stories.move: Profitable unit economics early, so no term sheet was ever needed.
stories.name: Zerodha: keeping control by not raising
stories.what: Zerodha was founded in 2010 and has never raised external capital. It grew into one of India’s largest brokers while profitable; Nithin Kamath has said bootstrapping gives freedom from chasing growth.

stories.apply: Keep clean records of every payment and approval; respond fully to board information requests; get independent counsel the moment an investigation starts.
stories.lesson: If you cannot produce documents quickly when the board asks, you lose the argument regardless of the merits.
stories.move: Weak documentation and a breakdown of trust with the board left the founder unable to defend herself in the board’s process.
stories.name: Zilingo: CEO terminated after investor probe
stories.what: After an anonymous whistleblower complaint, Zilingo’s board commissioned an investigation by Kroll and in 2022 terminated CEO Ankiti Bose, citing insubordination and failure to produce documents. She said the termination was wrongful. The company did not recover.

traps.ask: Founder seats tied to holding thresholds, independent directors chosen jointly, and a cap on total investor seats.
traps.clause: Board composition that flips at the next round
traps.india: Write board rights into the articles; removal of a director as such is not oppression (Tata v Mistry).
traps.looks: “Board: 2 founders, 1 Series A. Each future lead investor may appoint one director.”
traps.risk: After two more rounds investors hold the majority and can remove the CEO.

traps.ask: Drag needs founder or common-majority consent, a minimum price or return for common, and no drag within an initial period.
traps.clause: Drag-along with a low threshold and no price floor
traps.india: Put the drag in the articles (Rangaraj) and check FEMA pricing for resident sellers to non-residents.
traps.looks: “Holders of a majority of preferred shares may require all shareholders to sell on the same terms.”
traps.risk: Investors alone can force a sale at a price that only clears their preferences.

traps.ask: 30–45 days, falling away if the investor changes terms; costs capped and payable only if you walk away.
traps.clause: Long exclusivity or no-shop with costs
traps.india: These clauses are usually binding even in an otherwise non-binding term sheet; read which clauses are binding.
traps.looks: “The Company shall not solicit other investors for 90 days and shall reimburse the Investor’s legal costs if the transaction does not close.”
traps.risk: Locks you out of other offers while the investor can walk away or re-price.

traps.ask: A schedule of permitted existing ventures, freedom for non-competing businesses, and a time commitment rather than total exclusivity.
traps.india: Valid while you are engaged (Golikari, 1967); post-exit non-competes are void under s.27 (Percept D’Mark, 2006).
traps.looks: “Each Promoter shall devote full time to the Company and shall not be involved in any other business.”
traps.risk: Blocks you from starting or running your other ventures; breach can be a Cause event.

traps.ask: Broad-based weighted-average anti-dilution, with carve-outs for ESOP grants and small issues.
traps.india: Adjustments work through the conversion ratio of CCPS; check the result still meets FEMA pricing rules for foreign investors.
traps.looks: “If shares are later issued below the Series A price, the Series A conversion price is reduced to that price.”
traps.risk: One small down round reprices the investor’s whole stake to the new low price, transferring a large chunk of equity from founders.

traps.ask: 1x non-participating preference: the investor takes the higher of its money back or its pro-rata share, not both.
traps.india: Preferences are contractual and applied through the SHA and articles in a sale; on a winding up, creditors are paid first under the Companies Act or IBC.
traps.looks: “On a liquidation event, Series A receives 2x its investment and then participates pro rata with common.”
traps.risk: In a modest sale the investor takes its money back (or a multiple) and also a share of the rest, so founders and employees can get little or nothing even at a decent price.

traps.ask: Warranties from the company only; any founder warranty limited to title to your own shares and capped (for example, at a fraction of what you receive).
traps.india: Indian SSAs commonly add promoters as warrantors; resist it or cap it.
traps.looks: “The Company and the Promoters jointly and severally represent, warrant and indemnify…”
traps.risk: You personally pay if a warranty about the company proves wrong, often without any cap.
traps.seen: Byju’s founders’ personal acknowledgements of the loan default were cited by lenders.

traps.ask: Size the pool to an actual 12–18 month hiring plan, or let it sit in the post-money.
traps.clause: Option pool counted in the pre-money (‘pool shuffle’)
traps.india: Startups can grant ESOPs to promoters for 10 years from incorporation; decide whether founders draw from the same pool.
traps.looks: “Pre-money valuation includes an unallocated ESOP pool of 15% of the post-money capital.”
traps.risk: The new pool dilutes only existing holders, so the real price you get is lower than the headline valuation.

traps.ask: Company-level, best-efforts exit obligations only; no personal liability; exit at fair value.
traps.clause: Investor put option or buyback obligation on the promoters
traps.india: FEMA bars assured returns to foreign investors and requires at least a one-year lock-in before an option is exercised, but exit promises are still enforced (Nagaraj Mylandla, 2026).
traps.looks: “If no IPO or strategic sale occurs within five years, the Promoters shall purchase the Investor’s shares at an IRR of 15%.”
traps.risk: Turns equity into personal debt for the founders, enforceable through arbitration.

traps.ask: No redemption; any deadline should trigger only best-efforts liquidity steps, such as a secondary sale.
traps.clause: Redemption rights or an IPO deadline
traps.india: Redeemable instruments are treated as debt for foreign investors under FEMA, which is why Indian deals use compulsorily convertible preference shares.
traps.looks: “If a Qualified IPO does not occur within six years, investors may require redemption or a drag sale.”
traps.risk: Creates a forced exit on the investor’s timetable, regardless of market conditions.

traps.ask: Limit vetoes to changes in share rights, new senior securities, sale of the company, related-party deals and changes of business; set thresholds that scale.
traps.india: Courts uphold affirmative rights written into the articles (Tata v Mistry, 2021), so negotiate them before signing.
traps.looks: A schedule of 40 actions needing the Series A investor’s consent, including the annual budget, hiring above a salary, and any new contract above a small amount.
traps.risk: One investor can freeze the business or extract concessions at every decision.

traps.ask: Credit for time served, acceleration on termination without cause or on a sale, and a narrow, objective definition of Cause (fraud, wilful misconduct, conviction).
traps.clause: Founder vesting reset and broad ‘bad leaver’
traps.india: Leaver transfers need the articles to authorise them and FEMA pricing if a non-resident is involved.
traps.looks: “Founder shares vest over four years from closing. A founder terminated for Cause is a Bad Leaver and must sell all shares at the lower of cost and fair value.”
traps.risk: Restarting vesting on shares you already earned, and a vague ‘Cause’, let the board take back your equity cheaply after firing you.
traps.seen: BharatPe and Zilingo show how quickly boards act once misconduct is alleged.

quiz.q: Under the DPIIT notification of 4 February 2026, what is the turnover ceiling for a regular (non-deep-tech) startup?
quiz.why: It rose from ₹100 crore to ₹200 crore; ₹300 crore applies to Deep Tech Startups.

quiz.q: How long can a Deep Tech Startup keep its recognition after incorporation?
quiz.why: The 2026 framework gives deep-tech entities up to 20 years.

quiz.q: For how long after incorporation may a startup grant ESOPs to its promoters?
quiz.why: Rule 12 allows startups to grant ESOPs to promoters and directors holding more than 10% for up to 10 years from incorporation.

quiz.q: What is the minimum convertible note a DPIIT-recognised startup may accept in a single tranche?
quiz.why: At least ₹25 lakh in one tranche, repayable or convertible within 10 years.

It was a restraint of trade
quiz.q: In V.B. Rangaraj (1992), why was the family transfer restriction unenforceable?
quiz.why: Transfer restrictions bind the company and shareholders only if contained in the articles.

opts: Void under section 27 of the Contract Act
Valid if the founder is paid garden leave for two years
quiz.q: A founder’s agreement bars them from joining a competitor for two years after leaving. Under Indian law this is generally…
quiz.why: Post-termination restraints are void (Superintendence v Krishan Murgai; Percept D’Mark v Zaheer Khan).

opts: They are inadmissible until stamped but not void
quiz.q: What did the seven-judge bench decide in December 2023 about unstamped agreements with arbitration clauses?
quiz.why: In re Interplay overruled N.N. Global: the defect is curable and the arbitration clause survives.

opts: Refused to enforce a SIAC award as against public policy
Enforced a Singapore award on an investor-exit dispute and recognised transnational issue estoppel
Held SHAs governed by Indian law cannot be arbitrated abroad
Sent the dispute to the NCLT
quiz.q: In Nagaraj V. Mylandla v PI Opportunities Fund-I (2026), the Supreme Court…
quiz.why: It upheld enforcement and declined a disguised review of the tribunal’s reading of the SHA.

quiz.q: Which instrument counts as an equity instrument for foreign investment under the NDI Rules?
quiz.why: Only fully and mandatorily convertible instruments count; optionally convertible ones are debt.

opts: All Chinese investment via the automatic route
Investors outside land-border countries with up to 10% non-controlling LBC beneficial ownership to use the automatic route
Automatic route for Pakistan-based investors up to 26%
quiz.q: What did the March 2026 amendment to Press Note 3 allow?
quiz.why: Direct investors from land-border countries still need approval.

quiz.q: Within how many days must a company file Form FC-GPR after allotting shares to a foreign investor?
quiz.why: FC-GPR is due within 30 days of allotment.

opts: 25% of paid-up capital and free reserves
quiz.q: What is the maximum size of a buyback under section 68 of the Companies Act (current law)?
quiz.why: 25% of paid-up capital plus free reserves; the 2026 Bill would let prescribed classes exceed it.

opts: Only through a full NCLT scheme
Through the fast-track route under section 233 with Regional Director approval
It cannot merge; only a share swap is allowed
quiz.q: Since 17 September 2024, how can a foreign holding company merge into its wholly owned Indian subsidiary?
quiz.why: Rule 25A(5) of the merger rules opened the fast-track route for reverse flips.

opts: Unlimited layers with RBI approval only
quiz.q: Under Rule 19(3) of the Overseas Investment Rules, 2022, round-tripping structures are allowed up to…
quiz.why: No financial commitment is allowed if it results in more than two layers of subsidiaries.

opts: None if it is incorporated in Delaware
It may be Indian-resident because its place of effective management is in India
It loses its US tax status
quiz.q: A foreign holdco of an Indian startup is managed day to day from Bengaluru. What tax risk arises?
quiz.why: POEM in India makes a foreign company resident in India for income tax.

quiz.q: About how much tax did PhonePe’s investors pay to move its domicile from Singapore to India, according to its CEO?
quiz.why: Sameer Nigam said investors paid almost ₹8,000 crore in taxes.

quiz.q: Under the Income-tax Act, 2025, which section replaces the old section 80-IAC startup deduction?
quiz.why: 80-IAC maps to section 140; section 119 covers loss carry-forward on change in shareholding.

opts: Any 3 consecutive years out of the first 10
quiz.q: The startup tax holiday gives 100% deduction for…
quiz.why: Any three consecutive years within the first ten; 10-of-15 is the IFSC holiday.

quiz.q: From 1 April 2026, what is the effective tax rate on buyback gains for a non-corporate promoter?
quiz.why: Capital gains plus the promoter add-on gives 30% for non-corporate promoters and 22% for corporate promoters.

opts: A Mauritius TRC conclusively secures treaty exemption
Grandfathered pre-2017 investments are always exempt
GAAR can apply to a post-2017 exit from a pre-2017 investment lacking substance
quiz.q: What did the Supreme Court hold in Tiger Global (January 2026)?
quiz.why: The structure was an impermissible avoidance arrangement; the gains were taxable in India.

quiz.q: For which assessment year onward was the angel tax (s.56(2)(viib)) abolished?
quiz.why: Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 made it inapplicable from AY 2025-26, i.e. shares issued from FY 2024-25.

quiz.q: When do most DPDP obligations (notice, consent, security, breach reporting) start?
quiz.why: 13 May 2027, 18 months after the Rules; 13 November 2026 was consent-manager registration.

quiz.q: Under the labour codes, when does a fixed-term employee become eligible for gratuity?
quiz.why: One year of service, compared with five for permanent employees.

opts: A court order or government notification
An email from a rights holder
quiz.q: In Shreya Singhal (2015), ‘actual knowledge’ that ends an intermediary’s safe harbour means…
quiz.why: The Court read section 79 narrowly to protect platforms from private takedown pressure.

quiz.q: Under the Companies Act rules, shares with differential voting rights may carry at most what share of total voting power?
quiz.why: Rule 4 of the Share Capital Rules caps DVR voting power at 74%; SEBI’s SR framework uses the same ceiling.

opts: The Long-Term Benefit Trust via Class T stock
quiz.q: In Anthropic’s structure as reported from its 2026 IPO filing, who elects a majority of the board?
quiz.why: The co-founders’ Class F stock carries the majority of the general vote, but the Trust elects the board majority.

opts: Minority shareholders sued in Delaware and trial was days away
quiz.q: Why did Facebook drop its non-voting Class C share plan in 2017?
quiz.why: The plan was withdrawn before Zuckerberg was due to testify in the Court of Chancery.

quiz.q: A Series A term sheet gives the investor ‘2x participating’ preference. In a sale just above the money invested, founders typically…
quiz.why: The investor takes 2x first and then shares in the rest.

opts: Disqualification as a director of other companies for five years
quiz.q: You run three startups. One fails to file annual returns for three consecutive years. What can happen to you?
quiz.why: Section 164(2) of the Companies Act.

opts: A golden share held by a trust
quiz.q: Which founder protection does the Zerodha story illustrate best?
quiz.why: Bootstrapped and profitable, the founders never had to give up control in a term sheet.

quiz.q: Why do founders form a company instead of trading in their own name?
opts: It is a separate legal person, so owners' risk is usually limited
quiz.why: Limited liability: the company owns its debts, so owners usually lose only what they put in.

quiz.q: A company has 200 shares. You hold 50. What do you own?
An investor puts in ₹1 crore at a ₹4 crore pre-money valuation. What stake do they get?
quiz.why: Post-money = ₹5 crore; ₹1 crore ÷ ₹5 crore = 20%.

quiz.q: Which document is the company's official rulebook filed with the MCA?
quiz.why: The articles bind the company and all shareholders, so key SHA rights are copied into them.

quiz.q: Where does a shareholder complaint of unfair treatment (oppression) usually go?
quiz.why: The National Company Law Tribunal hears oppression and mismanagement cases.

quiz.q: You sell shares for more than you paid. What is the profit called for tax?
quiz.why: Profit on selling an asset like shares is a capital gain.

quiz.q: A brand bars its dealers from giving more than a 5% discount and fines those who do. What is the main legal risk?
opts: None: brands may control their dealers
Resale price maintenance under section 3(4) of the Competition Act
A breach of the Companies Act
quiz.why: Enforcing resale prices or discount caps is resale price maintenance. The CCI fined Maruti ₹200 crore for this in August 2021.

quiz.q: Under the Competition Act, below-cost 'predatory' pricing is illegal only when…
opts: a dominant enterprise uses it to reduce competition or eliminate competitors
prices are lower than a competitor's
quiz.why: Predatory pricing is a form of abuse of a dominant position under section 4; a non-dominant startup's launch discounts are not caught.

quiz.q: Under the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020, how quickly must a platform's grievance officer acknowledge a complaint?
quiz.why: Acknowledge within 48 hours; redress within one month.

quiz.q: Which of these cannot be patented in India under section 3(k)?
quiz.why: Section 3(k) excludes mathematical or business methods, computer programmes per se and algorithms. Software with a technical effect can still qualify.

quiz.q: Why couldn't BookMyShow stop 'bookmysports' in 2017?
opts: 'BOOKMY' described online booking and had not acquired distinctiveness
It sued in the wrong court
quiz.why: The Delhi High Court found the prefix descriptive and in use by others, so no single business could monopolise it.

quiz.q: How long does an Indian patent last?
quiz.why: Patents last 20 years. Trademarks last 10 years but can be renewed indefinitely; copyright in literary works lasts for life plus 60 years.

quiz.q: Which ad line is safest under Indian comparative-advertising law?
opts: 'Our soap is the best you can buy'
'Doctors say Brand X is unsafe' (no survey)
quiz.why: Puffery about your own product is allowed; unproven or denigrating statements about a rival are not.

quiz.q: After the Supreme Court's order of 7 May 2024 in the Patanjali case, what must an advertiser do before an ad runs?
opts: Submit a self-declaration that the ad complies with the rules
Pay a deposit to the CCPA
quiz.why: A self-declaration, on the lines of Rule 7 of the Cable Television Networks Rules, 1994, must be submitted before the ad is printed, aired or displayed.

quiz.q: A checkout adds a 'convenience fee' only on the last screen. Which specified dark pattern is this?
quiz.why: Drip pricing is revealing charges late in the purchase journey; it is one of the 13 patterns specified on 30 November 2023.

quiz.q: A customer paid ₹1.2 crore for a defective machine for personal use. Which consumer commission hears the complaint?
quiz.why: Since the December 2021 rules: District up to ₹50 lakh, State above ₹50 lakh and up to ₹2 crore, National above ₹2 crore.

quiz.q: Your consumer terms send all disputes to arbitration. Can a customer still file a consumer complaint?
opts: Yes, as held in Emaar MGF v Aftab Singh (2018)
quiz.why: The Supreme Court held that an arbitration clause does not take away the consumer's statutory remedy.

quiz.q: Under the MSMED Act, the longest payment period a buyer can agree with a micro or small supplier is…
quiz.why: Section 15 caps the agreed period at 45 days from acceptance; with no agreement, payment is due in 15 days.
