glossary.plain: A young company trying to grow fast with a new product or idea. In India the government (DPIIT) can officially 'recognise' a company as a startup, which unlocks some special rules and benefits.

Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade. The central government department that runs Startup India, decides which companies count as recognised startups, and frames India's foreign-investment policy.
An official 'yes, you are a startup' from DPIIT. You apply online; once approved, the company can use startup-only relaxations in company and tax law.
All the money a business earns from sales in a year, before taking away any costs. It is not the same as profit.
The official birth of a company: the day it is registered with the government and gets its certificate. Many startup rules count years 'from incorporation'.
A business the law treats as its own 'person'. It can own things, sign contracts, borrow and be sued in its own name, separately from the people who own it.
The usual startup structure in India. Owners hold shares, each owner's risk is limited to what they put in, and shares cannot be offered to the general public. Investors expect this form.
A business owned by 'partners' whose personal risk is limited. Simpler to run than a company, but it cannot issue shares, so it does not suit venture capital or share-based ESOPs.
A company with just one owner. Handy for testing an idea alone; it can later convert into a regular private company.
A legal category for smaller private companies (below set limits of capital and turnover). They get lighter paperwork, such as fewer required board meetings.
The money shareholders have actually paid the company for its shares.
One small unit of ownership in a company. If there are 100 shares and you own 10, you own 10% of the company.
Anyone who owns shares in a company, and so owns part of it. Shareholders vote on big decisions and appoint the directors.
Ownership in a company, usually as shares. 'Giving up equity' means handing over part of the ownership, often in exchange for money.
Shares that get certain priorities over ordinary shares, such as being paid back first if the company is sold or closed. Investors usually take these.

Compulsorily Convertible Preference Shares: preference shares that must turn into ordinary shares later. The standard way VC money enters Indian startups, because the rules treat them as ownership, not as a loan.
Compulsorily Convertible Debentures: loan-like papers that must turn into shares later, so the rules treat them as ownership.
A formal IOU a company issues to borrow money, usually paying interest.
A right to buy shares later at a price fixed today.

Employee Stock Option Plan: a promise that lets employees buy company shares later at a fixed, usually low, price. If the company grows, the options become valuable, so they reward people for staying.
The waiting period before you truly earn your shares or options. Options might 'vest' bit by bit over four years; leave early and you keep only the part that has vested.
Shares given to founders, directors or employees for their work, know-how or ideas instead of cash. You 'pay' for the shares with your sweat.
The people who started or control a company, usually the founders. Many Indian rules put extra duties, limits or taxes on promoters.
A person who started the company.
A member of the company's board. Directors oversee how the company is run and owe it legal duties of loyalty and care. Shareholders appoint them.
The group of directors that oversees the company. The board can hire and fire the CEO, so whoever controls the board really controls the company.
A board member with no money or family ties to the company or its founders, there to keep decisions fair.
The top executive who runs the company day to day (in India often called the Managing Director). The board appoints and can remove them.
Money an investor puts in now as a kind of loan that later turns into shares instead of being repaid. It lets a startup raise money before agreeing a valuation.
Money a company takes from people that it must repay. Company law controls deposits tightly; some startup instruments are exempt.
Selling new shares to a small, chosen group of people rather than to the public.
Issuing new shares to specific chosen people at a set price, with shareholder approval and an official valuation.
Offering new shares to existing shareholders first, in proportion to what they already own.
A shareholder decision that needs a bigger majority than usual (at least three times as many votes for as against). Used for important changes.
A professional registered with the government to put an official price on a company's shares.
What the whole company is considered to be worth. If an investor pays ₹1 crore for 10%, the company is being valued at ₹10 crore.
Pre-money is the company's value just before new investment comes in; post-money is the value just after (pre-money plus the new money).
When a company issues new shares, everyone else's percentage shrinks even though they still hold the same number of shares. That shrinking is dilution.
The list of who owns how many shares and what percentage of the company.
Someone who puts money into the company in exchange for shares (or a right to shares), hoping to earn more later.
Money from investment funds that back young, risky companies in exchange for shares, hoping a few become very large.
A wealthy individual who invests their own money in very early startups.
One fundraising event in which investors buy new shares. Rounds usually go Seed, then Series A, Series B and so on, each at a (hopefully) higher valuation.
When investors or founders turn their shares into cash: by selling the company, listing it (IPO), or selling shares back to the company or to new investors.

The contract between a company's shareholders (founders and investors) setting out who controls what, how shares can be sold, and what rights investors get. An SSA is the related contract for buying the new shares.
The company's official rulebook, filed with the government. Rules written into the articles bind the company and every shareholder, which is why investors want their rights copied into them.
A short summary of the main deal terms an investor offers, agreed before the full legal documents are written. Mostly non-binding, except clauses like exclusivity and confidentiality.
Before you sell your shares to an outsider, certain people (often investors) get the chance to buy them on the same terms first.
If a big shareholder sells, smaller shareholders can 'tag along' and sell their shares on the same terms.
Lets a majority of shareholders force everyone else to sell too, so a buyer can get 100% of the company.
A period during which shares cannot be sold.
A list of company decisions that need a particular shareholder's (usually an investor's) approval. In practice it gives them a veto.
National Company Law Tribunal: a special court for company-law disputes (like fights between shareholders) and for company insolvency cases.
National Company Law Appellate Tribunal: where you appeal against NCLT decisions. Above it is the Supreme Court.
A complaint to the NCLT by shareholders that the company is being run unfairly against them (oppression) or badly (mismanagement).
A private way to settle a dispute outside court. Both sides agree in their contract to let chosen arbitrators decide; the decision (an 'award') can be enforced like a court judgment.
The legal 'home' of an arbitration: the country whose courts supervise it. A Singapore-seated arbitration is overseen by Singapore's courts even if hearings happen elsewhere.
Singapore International Arbitration Centre: a popular institution that runs arbitrations. Many Indian startup investment contracts choose it.
A temporary arbitrator appointed within days to give urgent orders, before the full panel of arbitrators is set up.
The final decision in an arbitration, like a judgment. A 'foreign award' is one from an arbitration seated outside India.
One of the few reasons an Indian court can refuse to enforce an arbitration award: roughly, that it offends the basic principles of Indian law or justice. Courts read it narrowly.
A tax paid on many documents, such as agreements. An unstamped document cannot be used as evidence in court until the duty (and any penalty) is paid.
Someone who did not sign a contract. Sometimes a related company can still be bound by it.
A rule that a company in the same group as a signatory can be bound by its arbitration agreement if everyone's conduct shows that was intended.
A rule that stops a party from re-arguing a point a court has already decided against it. 'Transnational' means a decision by one country's court is respected in another country.
A clause stopping someone from working for, or starting, a competing business. In India, ones that apply after you leave are generally void.
A clause stopping someone from luring away the company's customers or staff.
Any agreement that stops someone from doing a lawful job or business. Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act makes these void, with narrow exceptions.
A notice period where an employee is still paid but told to stay away from work, which keeps them away from competitors for a while.
Things created by the mind that the law protects: code, designs, brand names, inventions and written work.
Legal ownership of original creative work, including software code. It decides who may copy or use it.
A written transfer of rights, such as IP, from one person to another.
Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023: India's main law on how businesses must collect, use and protect people's personal data.
Any information about an identifiable person: name, phone number, location, purchase history and so on.
The business that decides why and how personal data is used. 'Significant' data fiduciaries have extra duties.
The person the personal data is about: your user or customer.
A registered platform that lets people give, track and withdraw their consent to share personal data.
The official body under the DPDP Act that looks into data breaches and can impose penalties.
Four laws that replaced India's many older labour laws, covering wages, workplace relations, social security, and health and safety.
A lump sum an employer must pay an employee who leaves after a qualifying period of service, based on salary and years worked.
A retirement savings scheme where employer and employee each put in a share of salary every month.
Someone hired for a set period, such as one year, rather than indefinitely.
People who earn per task through apps, such as delivery riders and drivers, rather than as regular employees.
A platform company that connects customers with gig workers, like ride-hailing or delivery apps.
A platform that hosts or passes on other people's content or products: marketplaces, social apps, hosting services.
Legal protection that stops a platform being blamed for what its users post or sell, as long as it follows the rules and acts when officially told to.
Information Technology Act, 2000: India's main law on electronic records, cybercrime and online platforms.
Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999: the law that controls money moving into and out of India, including foreign investment in Indian companies. The RBI runs it day to day.
Reserve Bank of India, the country's central bank. It regulates banks and the foreign-exchange rules.
A foreign person or company putting money into an Indian company in exchange for shares.
Foreign investment that needs no government permission beforehand; you invest and report it afterwards.
Foreign investment that needs government permission before the money comes in.
A 2020 rule requiring government approval for investment from a country that shares a land border with India, or from someone whose real owner is from such a country.
A country that shares a land border with India, such as China, Pakistan, Bangladesh or Nepal. Investment linked to these countries faces extra checks.
The real person who ultimately owns or controls an investor, even when shares are held through other companies or funds.
Loans an Indian company takes from abroad, under separate and stricter rules than foreign investment in shares.
The price a share is properly worth, worked out using an approved method. Foreign-investment rules set minimum or maximum prices based on it.
The form a company files on the RBI's online portal to report shares issued to a foreign investor.
The form used to report a transfer of shares between someone living in India and someone living abroad.

Simple Agreement for Future Equity: a US-style contract where an investor pays now and gets shares later. It is not a recognised instrument under India's foreign-investment rules; Indian 'iSAFEs' are usually built as CCPS.
Someone who does not count as living in India for tax or foreign-exchange rules. An NRI is a non-resident Indian.
When a company buys its own shares back from shareholders, paying them cash.
Selling existing shares from one shareholder to another. The company gets no new money, unlike a 'primary' issue of new shares.
Profits the company has kept over the years that it is free to pay out.
Being able to turn something, like shares, into cash.
Moving a startup's top holding company abroad (often to Delaware or Singapore), so the Indian company becomes a subsidiary of a foreign parent.
Bringing the holding company back to India, usually before an Indian stock-market listing.
A company whose main job is owning shares in other companies. Holdco = holding company; opco = the operating company that actually runs the business.
A company owned or controlled by another company (its parent).
A US state whose company law and specialist business court are trusted by investors, so many startups set up their parent company there.
Place of Effective Management: where a company's key decisions are really made. If that is India, a foreign company can be taxed as an Indian one.
Selling shares of a foreign company whose value mostly comes from Indian assets. India can tax this as though the Indian assets themselves were sold.
Rules that make related companies price deals between themselves as if they were strangers, so profits cannot be shifted to low-tax countries.
An Indian person or company investing in a business abroad. Covered by the 2022 overseas-investment rules.
Money that leaves India and comes back in as 'foreign' investment through an offshore company.
Liberalised Remittance Scheme: the RBI scheme that caps how much money an Indian resident individual can send abroad each financial year.
Two companies combining into one. In a reverse flip, the foreign parent often merges into its Indian subsidiary.
A quicker merger process approved by a government official (the Regional Director) instead of a full tribunal hearing.
India's International Financial Services Centre in GIFT City, Gujarat. Businesses there are treated as 'offshore' for foreign-exchange rules and can get tax breaks. IFSCA is its regulator.
A period when a business's profits are fully or partly free of income tax.
The government panel that certifies which recognised startups can claim the startup tax holiday.
India's new income-tax law, which replaced the Income-tax Act, 1961 from 1 April 2026. Most section numbers changed.
Under the 2025 Act, the single April-to-March year whose income is taxed. It replaces the old pair of 'previous year' and 'assessment year'.
Under the old 1961 law, the year after you earned income, in which that income was assessed and taxed.
A non-cash benefit from your job, such as the gain when you exercise ESOPs, which is taxed like salary.
Using your option to actually buy the shares at the agreed price.
Profit from selling something like shares for more than you paid. Taxed separately from salary or business income; a capital loss is the opposite.
The normal income-tax rates that rise in steps as your income rises.
Raising the purchase price for inflation before working out a gain, which lowers the tax. No longer available for these share gains.
Using losses from past years to reduce tax on future profits.
A company not listed on a stock exchange and owned by a small group.
A share of the company's profits paid out to shareholders.
Money the tax law treats as a dividend even though the company did not formally declare one.
General Anti-Avoidance Rule: lets the tax department ignore a structure whose main purpose is to save tax and that has no real business reason behind it.
An agreement between two countries deciding which of them can tax which income, so people and companies are not taxed twice on the same money.
Official proof that a person or company is tax-resident in a country, needed to claim tax-treaty benefits.
Routing an investment through a country mainly to grab its tax-treaty benefits.
Letting older arrangements keep the old rules after a law changes.
Most-Favoured-Nation clause: a promise that if one country later gives someone else a better treaty deal, you get that deal too.
Tax the payer must cut from a payment and send to the government before paying the rest.
A payment for using someone else's IP, such as a licence to use copyrighted work.
A fixed place of business in a country, like an office or site, that lets that country tax a foreign company's profits made there.
Investors' right to get their money back (or a multiple of it) before founders and employees get anything when the company is sold or closed.
A participating preference lets investors take their money back AND a share of what is left. Non-participating means they choose the higher of the two, not both.
Protection that gives investors extra shares, or a lower conversion price, if the company later raises money at a lower price.
The harshest anti-dilution: the investor's whole price resets down to any lower later price.
A milder anti-dilution formula that only partly adjusts the investor's price, depending on how much cheaper money came in.
Shares set aside for future employee options.
Raising money at a lower valuation than the previous round.
A promise in a contract that certain facts are true. If they turn out false, the person who promised can owe money.
A promise to cover someone's losses if a particular thing goes wrong.
A personal promise to pay someone else's debt (for example, the company's) if they do not pay.
A right for an investor to force someone, often the founders, to buy their shares at an agreed price.
Internal Rate of Return: an investment's return expressed as a yearly percentage.
The company paying back an instrument, such as preference shares, in cash.
Initial Public Offering: when a company first sells shares to the public and gets listed on a stock exchange.
A promise not to talk to other investors or buyers for a period while one deal is being negotiated.
Shares with more (or fewer) votes per share than ordinary shares. They let founders keep control while owning less.
A rule that makes special rights expire after a set time or event.
A US company type that must balance making profit with a stated public purpose.
A share structure with two or more classes of shares carrying different numbers of votes.
A special share giving its holder the decisive say (often a veto) on key decisions.
When a company cannot pay its debts. Under India's Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, creditors can start a process that takes control away from the owners and the board.
The official who runs a company during insolvency, in place of its board.
The legal process when a person or company cannot pay its debts. Chapter 11 is the US process for restructuring a company while it keeps operating.
Closing a company and selling its assets to pay creditors; whatever is left goes to shareholders. In term sheets, a 'liquidation event' often also includes a sale of the company.
Someone the company owes money to.
Failing to keep a promise in a contract, such as not repaying a loan on time. 'Events of default' are listed triggers that let lenders demand money or take control.
A court decision against a party who did not properly take part in the case.
The pre-trial stage, common in US courts, where each side must hand over relevant documents and information.
A promise in a loan or investment contract to do, or not to do, certain things. A negative covenant is a promise not to do something.
A loan of a fixed amount repaid over a fixed period.
Being formally added as a party to a court case.
First Information Report: the document the police file to start a criminal investigation in India.
An investor's or buyer's detailed check of a company's accounts, contracts and legal position before investing.
A deal between the company and its own directors, founders, their relatives or their other companies. It needs special approvals because of the conflict of interest.
Insurance that protects directors and officers if they are personally sued over company decisions.
A person who reports wrongdoing inside an organisation.
An independent accountant who checks and certifies a company's accounts every year. A 'qualified opinion' means the auditor has reservations about them.
Ministry of Corporate Affairs: the government ministry that runs company law and the company registry where companies file their records.
Securities and Exchange Board of India: the regulator for stock markets, listed companies, IPOs and investment funds.
Central Board of Direct Taxes: the body that runs income tax in India.
Special Purpose Acquisition Company: a listed shell company that merges with a private company to take it public.
Delaware's specialist business court, which hears most US company-law disputes.
A legal duty to act in someone else's best interests, such as directors toward the company and its shareholders.
Building a company with your own money and its revenue instead of outside investors.
Whether you make or lose money on each single customer or sale.
Startups built on new science or engineering, such as AI, biotech or space, which usually take longer to build.
A former tax on unlisted companies that raised money above their shares' fair value. It has been abolished.
The amount investors pay for a share above its face (nominal) value.
The highest court of a country, or in the US of a state (e.g. the Delaware Supreme Court). In India, Supreme Court rulings bind every other court.
The top court of a state (or group of states), just below the Supreme Court.
An earlier court decision that later courts follow on the same legal question.
A court ruling that still applies today: it has not been overturned or replaced by a new law.
When a higher court decides an earlier ruling was wrong, so it no longer applies.
A court order telling someone to do, or stop doing, something.
Of no legal effect, as if it never existed. A void clause cannot be enforced.
Making a contract or ruling actually happen, with a court's backing.
A law passed by Parliament (an Act).
A law that also applies to past events, not just future ones.
A specialist body that decides certain kinds of disputes, much like a court.
A temporary order to protect someone until a case is finally decided.
Companies Act, 2013: the main law on how Indian companies are formed, owned and run.
Indian Contract Act, 1872: the basic law on agreements and when they can be enforced.
A numbered part of an Act. 's.27' is short for 'section 27'.
Someone who counts as living in a country for tax or foreign-exchange rules.
Goods and Services Tax: India's tax on the sale of most goods and services, separate from income tax.
What is left from income after paying all costs.
Money coming in from sales; same idea as turnover.
Indian number words: 1 lakh = 1,00,000 (one hundred thousand); 1 crore = 1,00,00,000 (ten million).
Forced out of a job or position, for example a founder removed as CEO by the board.
The rules and processes for how a company is controlled and decisions are made and checked.
Tax planning uses the law as written; avoidance uses artificial structures to dodge tax and can be struck down (GAAR); evasion is hiding income and is a crime.
Your plan for reaching paying customers: who you sell to first, what you tell them, where you find them, who does the selling and what you charge.
A description of the customer who needs your product most and can pay for it, such as 'clinics with 5 to 20 doctors in tier-2 cities'.
The first small market you aim to win completely before expanding, like landing on one beach before moving inland.
A way of selling where people try the product themselves (free trial or free plan) and upgrade without talking to a salesperson.
What you spend on marketing and sales to win one new paying customer.
The total profit you expect from one customer over the whole time they stay with you. It should be well above CAC.
The regulator that stops cartels, abuse of market power and harmful mergers under the Competition Act, 2002. It can impose large fines.
When a supplier forces dealers or resellers to sell at a fixed or minimum price, or caps their discounts. Can be illegal under the Competition Act.
Selling below cost to drive competitors out. Illegal in India only for a company that dominates the market.
Enough market power to act without worrying much about competitors or customers. Being dominant is legal; abusing it is not.
An online platform that connects independent buyers and sellers without owning the goods sold. The only e-commerce model open to foreign investment.
E-commerce where the platform owns the stock it sells. Foreign investment is not allowed in this model.
A name, logo, slogan, shape or colour combination that tells customers a product comes from you. Registration lasts 10 years and is renewable.
A court claim to stop someone making their business look like yours and stealing your goodwill. Works even for unregistered names.
Using a brand name before someone else used or registered it. Under section 34 of the Trade Marks Act it can protect your right to keep using it.
A brand name that just describes the product or service ('BookMy…', 'Fresh Juice'). Hard to protect unless the public links it only to you.
When a descriptive word has become so linked with one business that people think of it first. Then it can be protected.
The overall look of a product or store: colours, shapes, packaging and layout. Copying it can be passing off.
A trademark made of colours, like Louboutin's red sole. Indian law lets a combination of colours count as a mark.
A government-granted right to stop others making or using your invention for 20 years, in exchange for publishing how it works.
A real technical improvement, such as faster processing, less memory or better security, that can make a software-based invention patentable in India.
Extending a patent monopoly by patenting small changes to an existing product. Section 3(d) blocks this for drugs in India.
A first, simpler patent filing that secures your date. The complete specification must follow within 12 months.
Protection for how a product looks (shape, pattern, ornament) for 10 years, extendable by 5.
Valuable business information kept confidential, like a recipe or algorithm. Protected in India through contracts and breach-of-confidence claims.
India's test for copyright originality: effort alone isn't enough; there must be at least a little creative skill and judgment.
An ad that falsely describes a product, gives a false guarantee, or hides important information. The CCPA can fine advertisers and endorsers.
Obvious exaggerated praise of your own product ('the best in the world') that nobody takes as a literal fact. Allowed in ads.
Running down a competitor's product in an ad. Courts can order such ads taken down.
The national regulator under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 that acts against misleading ads, unfair trade practices and dark patterns.
A celebrity, influencer or expert who promotes a product. Endorsers can be fined or banned for misleading ads.
Advertising a banned product (like liquor) indirectly by promoting another product with the same brand name. Prohibited since 2022.
A website or app design that tricks people into doing something they didn't intend, like fake timers or hidden fees. 13 types are banned in India.
Showing a low price first and adding extra fees step by step, often only at checkout. A banned dark pattern.
A statement an advertiser must submit before an ad runs, confirming it follows the rules. Required since the Supreme Court's May 2024 order.
Special consumer courts (district, state and national) where buyers can complain cheaply about defective goods, poor service or unfair terms.
Contract terms that are heavily one-sided against a consumer. Consumer commissions can declare them void.
The legal duty of makers, sellers and service providers to compensate people harmed by defective products or deficient services.
The highest price a packaged product can be sold for in India, including all taxes. It must be printed on the pack.
Under the MSMED Act, 2006 buyers must pay micro and small suppliers within the agreed time, at most 45 days, or pay steep interest.
An amount fixed in a contract to be paid if someone breaches it. Courts treat it as a maximum and award reasonable compensation up to it.
A contract clause that limits how much one side has to pay if things go wrong, often to the fees paid.
A collection of colours, images and type that sets the look and feeling of a brand or campaign before design work starts.
